news.title: Trump ties, fraud crisis put Tafoya and Flanagan on defense in Senate debate
news.text:
Republican Michele Tafoya sought to establish her independence from President Donald Trump, while Democratic Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan faced questions about party loyalty and her responsibility for Minnesota’s fraud crisis during their first and only scheduled U.S. Senate debate Friday.

The debate came just days after Trump encouraged Minnesotans to vote for Tafoya. Flanagan used the event to cast the former sportscaster as someone who would be a rubber stamp for the president’s agenda. 

“Let’s be clear: Donald Trump doesn’t just endorse anybody. In fact, he endorses against people in his own party if they dare to take him on,” Flanagan said. “Michele Tafoya passed his litmus test with flying colors.” 

But Tafoya used the debate to highlight where she would break from her party and Trump, including on the Iran war. She also sought to turn the tables on Flanagan’s critique.

Advertisement

“I would challenge my opponent to tell us where and when she has ever parted with her own party, with the far left flank of her party, on any issue,” Tafoya said. 

Tafoya kept a distance from Trump throughout the debate and declined to say whether she wanted his endorsement or would campaign alongside him in Minnesota.

“My campaign is about including people from all along the political spectrum,” she said. “I invite Trump voters. I invite Kamala Harris voters.” 

Flanagan similarly declined to say whether she wanted Gov. Tim Walz to campaign with her as Republicans made his administration’s fraud crisis a central attack.
news.summary: The candidates challenged each other’s independence from their parties and split over tariffs, abortion and immigration enforcement in their only scheduled debate.
news.author: Allison Kite,Sydney Kashiwagi

news.title: Kamala defends her cackle, accuses critics of trying to steal her ‘joy’
news.text:
In a recent appearance on Keke Palmer’s podcast, Kamala Harris explained away her chilling laugh as an endearing family trait, before leaving the door wide open to yet another presidential campaign.

“I’m aware of the, whatever the memes are about, you know, my laugh. Well, look, I was raised in a family that included very powerful women who laughed from their bellies,” Kamala said.

“And powerful, I mean, they were powerful in their space. They were powerful in their family and their community, not necessarily titles and money. But you understand my point,” she continued, as Palmer nodded.

“And they would sit around the kitchen table with their coffee, laughing loud laughs, and that’s how I laugh. And the people that I respected laugh the same way,” she cackled.

Kamala continued, “And everybody else, you know what they can do,” before pivoting to discuss her “joy.”

“Those who try to take your joy are trying to make you weak. And that’s where my fight comes in. I know what you’re trying to do,” she added.

“What do we try to do?” BlazeTV host Pat Gray asks, genuinely confused.

Jeff Fisher notes that following Kamala’s mini-monologue on her laugh, Palmer responded to her that she was “so brave.”

“She grabbed a Kleenex and everything,” he adds.

But laughter isn’t all the pair discussed. In a follow-up clip, Palmer asked Kamala if she’ll be running for president in 2028.

Kamala laughed maniacally before answering, “I haven’t decided.”

Gray doesn’t believe her, commenting, “What a liar.”

“There’s no doubt in my mind she’s going to run,” he adds.

news.title: 'The View' co-hosts cast doubt on Kamala Harris viability as 2028 candidate
news.text: Several co-hosts of "The View" expressed doubts Friday about former Vice President Kamala Harris running for president in 2028. Harris was asked during a Tuesday interview with podcaster Keke Palmer whether she was considering running for president in 2028. Harris laughed and said she hadn't decided yet. However, some of "The View" co-hosts urged the Democratic Party to seek another contender. "Let’s be real," co-host Ana Navarro said, noting that she spoke with Harris about how many women remain "scarred" by the fact both she and former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton lost to President Donald Trump. When asked if a Black woman could be elected president, guest host Raven-Symone replied, "Not in America. In the days after Joe Biden dropped out in 2024, online platforms saw racist content directed at Kamala go up 525% and misogynistic content went up 2,328%." This would be her third time on this ballot from the first time when she didn’t — she was out really early when she ran, and then the time with Biden, this would be the third time." news.title: Nobody Wants To Be the Pro-Tech Candidate in This New York Race That Could Flip the House
news.text:
The Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) candidates running for the House of Representatives and endorsed by NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani are all but guaranteed to win their general elections this November, but that does not mean the midterm drama is over in New York. In the state's 17th congressional district, which includes the lower Hudson Valley, Democratic challenger Cait Conley, a combat veteran who served on the Biden administration's National Security Council, could unseat incumbent Republican congressman Mike Lawler in one of the most consequential races of the midterms. 

The highly contested purple district voted for former Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 election while reelecting Lawler for his second term. Now, Lawler is attempting to win a third term as support for President Donald Trump wanes ahead of the midterms. As of Friday, The Cook Political Report lists the race, which could determine control of the House, as a toss-up. 

If elected, Conley would have far more in common with the "Badass Women" coalition of security state and military veterans than with DSA types (think more Sen. Elissa Slotkin from Michigan than Darializa Avila Chevalier). As Judge Street Journal's Timmy Facciola notes, "Conley's candidacy is testing the viability of a tactful centrism that rebukes left-wing positions like abolishing ICE or restricting weapon shipments to Israel." Lawler is also vying for moderates, pitching himself as "one of the most bipartisan members of Congress" and emphasizing his willingness to break with Trump occasionally while still welcoming Trump's support. 

While Lawler and Conley certainly are not pure MAGA acolytes or DSA members, both have leaned into a tech-critical position, much like that of more radical populists like Lina Khan or Steve Bannon, revealing how pervasive anti-tech sentiment has become in mainstream politics. 

This tech skepticism was on full display during an October 14 debate, when each candidate made the case for why they were the most equipped to regulate AI, insisting that the industry needs guardrails. 

Conley said members of Congress do not want to regulate AI because "they want to look out for their billionaire and trillionaire backers like Elon Musk, who is pouring over $260 million into this midterm election." She then added that Musk backed Lawler in his 2024 race. 

Lawler then accused Conley, who previously consulted for Primer AI, of being "the AI candidate for the AI industry."

While Lawler and Conley disagree on specific data center regulations (Conley supports Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul's data center moratorium while Lawler supports local zoning control over data centers), neither wants to pitch themselves as an explicitly pro-data center candidate. During the debate, Conley claimed that, "On Mike Lawler's watch there have been five data centers built in Rockland County." Lawler has said that he had no say in the decision to build the data centers, and during the debate, he pointed out that the facilities were built for financial services. Lawler also attempted to attack Conley over data centers, slamming her in an ad for saying "we need data centers." Regardless of the candidates' specific policies on data centers, their attacks on one another demonstrate that cheerleading hyperscale data center development is a political liability. In their district, data center has presumably become a dirty term. 

The candidates' tech-skeptical rhetoric did not end with unchecked data center development. After the debate, Reason asked both candidates about their positions on age-verification laws for social media and AI, since such regulations raise significant privacy and censorship concerns by age-gating the internet. Unsurprisingly, both Lawler, who voted for the controversial KIDS Act, and Conley, who has proposed stricter age verification for AI tools, parroted platitudes about why such online safety regulations are necessary to protect children. 

"We have watched how social media is literally hurting the mental health of children," Conley told Reason. "And when you talk about the power of AI and what that power could do, we have to regulate this." 

Lawler gave a similar response, telling Reason that he respects free speech but that protecting children "is paramount." 

This bipartisan consensus over social media regulation has long been brewing in Congress. The mainstream political conversations about AI and data centers, however, are relatively new this midterm election cycle. And it appears both Lawler and Conley have figured out which way Americans' sentiment toward AI is leaning, and they have waged their campaigns accordingly.
news.summary: Republican incumbent Mike Lawler and Democratic challenger Cait Conley are trying to tie each other to the AI industry and data centers.
news.author: Meagan O'Rourke

news.title: Map Shows 14 GOP-Held House Seats Shifting Toward Democrats in Past Week
news.text: Republicans have been dealt another blow as data compiled from the Cook Political Report shows 14 U.S. House seats in 10 states currently held by Republicans are shifting toward Democrats 18 days before the November 3 midterm elections. Republicans are fighting to defend their razor-thin majorities in both chambers of Congress as voters weigh concerns about the economy, inflation, President Donald Trump's job performance and the ongoing U.S. war with Iran. The GOP currently holds a 218-214 edge in the House and a 53-47 majority in the Senate, leaving little room for losses in a midterm cycle that features a number of highly competitive races. Democrats have an opportunity to flip one or both chambers, including in several states that have traditionally leaned Republican. "Republicans remain laser-focused on winning, protecting and expanding President Trump’s House majority," Republican National Committee Press Secretary Natalie Baldassarre told Newsweek. "While Democrats celebrate political ratings, we’re thinking outside the box and pouring resources into battleground districts to highlight President Trump’s historic achievements, boost our candidates and defy history on November 3.” Newsweek reached out to the Democratic National Committee by email and the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee by phone for comment on Friday. Which House Races Are Shifting Democrat? On Friday, a Cook Political Report said that 11 House races are shifting toward Democrats, including five seats in four states held by Republicans. Of the five, all are still considered "lean R," according to Cook, but the move indicates that the results could be tighter than originally thought. Similarly, a report on October 9 showed nine House seats currently held by Republicans shifting toward Democrats, including traditionally Republican states that Trump won big in 2024. Despite the changes, several of the impacted states are still favored to have a Republican win. Minnesota Minnesota's First Congressional District, represented by Republican Brad Finstad, has shifted from "likely R" to "lean R." Finstad is facing Democrat Jake Johnson, with some polls showing the candidates tied. Trump won Finstad's district by 12 points in 2024. Ohio Ohio has two House seats occupied by Republicans—Mike Turner in the 10th District and Mike Carey in the 15th—that shifted from "likely R" to "lean R" this week. Turner is running against Democrat Kristina Knickerbocker, while Carey is up against Democrat Don Leonard. Trump won Ohio by nearly 12 points in 2024. When it comes to the Senate, the race between Republican Senator Jon Husted and Democratic former Senator Sherrod Brown is among a handful of toss-ups that could determine the balance of power. Kansas Kansas' 2nd Congressional District, represented by Republican Derek Schmidt, shifted from "solid R" to "likely R." The Democratic candidate is Don Coover. Trump won the district by 20 points in 2024. Nebraska Nebraska's 1st Congressional District seat, occupied by Republican Mike Flood, shifted from "solid R" to "likely R." The Democratic candidate is Chris Backemeyer. Trump won Nebraska by 20 points in 2024. Iowa Republicans Mariannette Miller-Meeks in the 1st district and Zach Nunn in the 3rd saw their races shift from "toss-up" to "lean D." In the 1st district, the Democratic candidate is Christina Bohannan, while Sarah Trone Garriott is running in the 3rd. Trump won Iowa for all three of his presidential campaigns, including by nearly 14 points in 2024. Iowa is also among the most competitive U.S. Senate races, with Republican Ashley Hinson and Democrat Josh Turek vying for retiring Republican Joni Ernst's seat. Pennsylvania Three of Pennsylvania's House seats currently occupied by Republicans showed changes as well. The races for the 7th and 10th congressional districts, held by Ryan Mackenzie and Scott Perry, respectively, were change from "toss-up" to "lean D" by Cook. The 1st Congressional District, held by Republican Brian Fitzpatrick, shifted from "likely R" to "lean R." Democrats running are: Bob Brooks (in the 7th District); Janelle Stelson, who is currently leading Perry in polls in the 10th; and Bucks County Commissioner Bob Harvie in the 1st. Trump won Pennsylvania by less than 2 points in 2024. Michigan Michigan's 4th Congressional District, held by Republican Bill Huizenga, moved from "lean R" to "toss-up" category. The Democratic candidate is state Senator Sean McCann. Trump won Michigan by 1.4 points in 2024. Michigan is also tight in the Senate race between Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers, a former congressman, to succeed retiring Democratic Senator Gary Peters. Virginia Virginia's 1st Congressional District, a seat held by Republican Rob Wittman, shifted from "lean R" to "toss-up." Democrat Shannon Taylor led Wittman by 4 points in a recent Washington Post poll. Trump lost Virginia to Kamala Harris by 5 points in 2024. Arkansas Arkansas' 2nd Congressional District, held by Republican French Hill, shifted from "solid R" to "likely R." The Democratic candidate is Chris Jones, a nuclear engineer who ran for governor in 2022. Trump won Arkansas by more than 30 points in 2024. Indiana Indiana's 5th Congressional District, held by Republican Victoria Spartz, shifted from "solid R" to "likely R." Spartz's Democratic opponent is state Senator JD Ford. Trump won Indiana by 19 points in 2024. What Happens Next In most states, early voting has begun and will continue up until Election Day on November 3. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Anna Skinner and Dave Siminoff.
news.summary: More than a dozen U.S. House seats in 10 states currently held by Republicans are shifting toward Democrats.
news.author: Anna Skinner

news.title: “History Will Judge”: Fox News Anchor Bret Baier on Donald Trump and Pete Hegseth’s War With the Press
news.text:
Tonight he’s on better behavior, waving off wine and sticking to soda water. “I have an election diet,” he tells me, explaining that he drops around 15 pounds every October of an election year. He recommends the beef tenderloin but orders the branzino for himself.
Tucked into a corner seat at the best table in the room, Baier is in his element. He pats down his hair, which is short and sculpted and appears totally immovable, like the top of a Playmobil figurine. He’s just come off set, and his face remains brushed with the tan makeup that ensures its uniformity and consistency through time and space and episodes of Special Report, the daily news program he has anchored for the last 17 years. The job—that is, serving as the face of the mighty conservative network’s news operation, which is celebrating its 30th year in business this month—has grown more challenging over the years as the institution has become increasingly intertwined with Donald Trump’s political movement.
We’re discussing the president’s attacks on the press, which recently culminated in an unprecedented attempt to ban certain news outlets from the White House over their coverage. “We made our feelings clear the second it happened,” Baier tells me. Privately, Baier lobbied Trump to reverse the ban, I’d been told by a source with knowledge of the conversations. Publicly, Fox News joined the rest of the media in pulling its coverage from the White House press pool. “There are die-hard MAGA folks who say that it was the wrong move, but there was no doubt,” he says. “There was never even a split second of thinking about it.”
It isn’t the only measure Fox is taking against the Trump administration: Internally, the network has for months paused booking interviews with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, a former Fox News host, following his ejection of journalists from the Pentagon. “I always had a good relationship with him at Fox,” Baier says of Hegseth. “Obviously, I’m not a proponent of what he did with the Pentagon press pool. And I see…[the president] talks about him all the time as central casting.”
I ask whether he would host Hegseth on Special Report. “If I get clearance to, I would,” he says. He’s not getting clearance right now? “No, I mean, I think we made another decision as a news organization once we left the premises and got kicked out, and that was the decision that was made.”
It’s an early taste of the anchorman’s studied posture of neutrality—though Baier does, for a moment, betray a point of view. “I hope he lets the press back in,” he says.
“I hate the tie,” he says.
“I know you hate the tie,” the producer responds.
In his second decade as anchor and executive editor, Baier has perfected the science of Special Report, Fox’s flagship news operation, which airs weekdays at 6 p.m. and is run with a fierce efficiency. There are around three crew members on set at any given time, and another 10 staffers sit in a control room, a whirring hub managing a network of foreign and domestic correspondents who beam in for quick hits.
“Honestly, I hate the tie,” Baier says, fixated. “It screws up the tie.”
The microphone remains on the tie. A producer begins the countdown to live, and at exactly 6 p.m., Baier looks up from his laptop for the first time since sitting down and says amiably into the camera: “Good evening, and welcome to Washington. I’m Bret Baier.”
In the first block of the show, he throws to a correspondent in Paris covering the riots there, then to the State Department, the White House, and Ithaca, New York, for a dispatch on the protests at Cornell University. In 10 minutes, Special Report has covered five stories. In a final segment, a panel featuring three national political reporters weighs in on the upcoming midterms. By the end, this precisely choreographed endeavor produces an hour of television that draws an average of more than 2.5 million viewers each night, which makes Special Report the most watched hard-news program in all of cable.
These days, Baier measures his success against that of the broadcast networks—CBS, ABC, NBC—which he beats in some key markets. But he remembers when his ambitions were considerably more modest. “I went around doing stories and I’d say I was with Fox, and they’d say, ‘Is that the Simpsons network?’” he says. “And so the prospect of us beating a big [broadcast] network that still has much further reach is really pretty amazing.”
Seventeen years and a few dollars later, Baier now divides his time between Washington, where he still spends three to four nights a week, and a large home he recently purchased in Palm Beach, a short drive from Mar-a-Lago. He sold his house in the capital, a mansion in leafy Foxhall inspired by a Loire Valley château, to Howard Lutnick, Trump’s billionaire commerce secretary. “He got a good deal,” Baier says.
Baier’s rise to television stardom began by violent chance. He was an industrious correspondent in Fox’s Atlanta bureau when the first plane hit the World Trade Center on September 11, 2001, and he was called to the network’s New York City headquarters to help cover the attack. “We started driving, and then the third plane hit the Pentagon,” he says. “They rerouted us.” He drove from Georgia to Arlington, Virginia. “I started doing live shots for Fox affiliates outside the burning Pentagon that night, and I never left.” He was soon named Fox’s Pentagon correspondent, traveling frequently to Iraq and Afghanistan. In 2009 he took over Special Report from his mentor, Brit Hume, who offered three simple pieces of advice to the young newsman: “The show is not about you, the show is not about you, and let the news drive the show.”
Back then, Baier faced stiff competition within the network from straight-news anchors like Chris Wallace and Shepard Smith. But Trump’s rise to power ushered in changes at Fox News, which has seen the news hours on its schedule shrink, replaced by opinion shows, which tend to draw stronger ratings. “The landscape changed,” Baier says. “There’s a lot more opinion programming overall in the cable universe.” In this uncertain new world, Baier has established himself as the face of Fox’s news operation, the man called upon to moderate presidential debates and interview world leaders.
When it comes to foreign heads of state, it can sometimes feel like Special Report is their first stop in Washington. “I’d like to say it’s because the booking is really good,” Baier says with a laugh. “When you have big foreign leaders appear one after another, they line up like planes at Dulles.” There’s also the matter of who’s watching. “I hear they also want to talk to a viewer, a particular one who watches Special Report,” Baier adds. Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy, amid a yearslong bid to convince Trump to support his cause, has appeared seven times.
Special Report’s most important viewer has a fraught relationship with the show and its host. Trump has lashed out at Baier before, calling him “nasty” after the Fox anchor pointed out in an interview that Trump lost the 2020 election. But Baier maintains a good relationship with the president, who often calls to talk off the record, sometimes to complain. Baier recalls one example, deploying a perfect Trump impression: “‘Bret, I tell you what, you’re a six. You’re not a seven or an eight. You’re a six.’” Baier says he replied, “I’ll take six. I’m pretty close to five. I’m doing good.”
During a book party that Baier hosted for Sylvester Stallone earlier this month, he pulled his phone out and said there was someone who wanted to talk to the actor. It was Trump, who had called to offer well-wishes. The anchor and the president have also golfed together, which critics say betrays a coziness between the scandal-plagued president and the newsman. “Look, if you had three hours with the leader of the free world where you could pick his brain off the record while you’re playing a sport,” Baier says, “I would take that with any president.”
Yet Baier’s critics question his claim to impartiality—citing, beyond the network’s overall reputation, a few high-profile incidents. In 2016 he issued a correction and an apology after inaccurately reporting, days before the election, that Hillary Clinton would be indicted. And during the 2024 campaign, Baier interrogated Vice President Kamala Harris in a manner some viewers found aggressive, with the host interrupting her at points—though Baier would later contend that Harris came into the interview looking for a fight.
Like any anchor, Baier is determined to give little away, and he carries a politico’s devotion to staying on message. When he’s questioned about the other activities of the network that employs him, he says he maintains “horse blinders” on his show. This is not entirely true, of course. He follows the controversies and outrages and scandals provoked (and stoked) by the rest of the network and has privately expressed frustrations with some of its coverage, according to one person who knows him personally. In 2020, as some Fox hosts promoted Trump’s false claims about the election, Baier fumed about the coverage on Maria Bartiromo’s show, according to internal communications revealed as part of a lawsuit at the time. He does not share any of this with me.
“Friends with Maria,” he says when I ask about her abrupt ouster from the network over the summer. “Great lady. Didn’t have any specifics when it all went down. Still really don’t have the whole picture”—and then we’re interrupted by the Trump adviser Jason Miller, who has come over to say hello.
When I continue my questioning about his Fox colleagues and reach Mark Levin, the cantankerous windbag who recently defended Trump’s media ban even as the rest of the network fought against it, Baier demurs again. “Again, my day is with literally horse blinders on from six to seven,” he says.
“But you don’t really have horse blinders on,” I note. “You watch this stuff.”
“I don’t actually watch it,” he says. “But obviously I see clips and I hear it. Does it bother me? No, because you know what? There’s an opinion page and a news page. They’re opinion folks. They do a great job at what they do. We’re rowing the same way for the company, but it’s a different job.”
This zone defense has been honed through years of sitting with journalists like me, answering questions like this. “Do you ask this question to NBC when they go crazy on their opinion programs?” he asks. I assure him that I would. “Fox is under the spotlight a lot, and always has been,” he continues. “I get asked about opinion folks all the time, and I’m fine with it. I don’t see a lot of stories that scrutinize what the opinion people on other channels are saying.”
The Trump era is different, of course. The false information the president demands his supporters endorse is of a magnitude not seen in modern times—a reality well-known to Fox given the costly defamation lawsuits the network faced over Trump’s election lies. Amid the 2020 chaos, Baier fact-checked false claims about the election on his show. But as the network faced a viewer revolt over its election desk’s call that Joe Biden won the state of Arizona, he reportedly suggested that the network “pull” the call and “put it back in [Trump’s] column.” (In a statement at the time, Baier said his comments were taken out of context. Some analysts, including Nate Silver, had argued Fox should retract their call—which ended up being correct.) Baier’s sign-off on Special Report is “Fair, balanced, and unafraid,” but that motto sounds more strained than ever in a time with rampant misinformation and growing audience pressures, not to mention a press corps treated with hostility and distance.
When Baier introduced the report on the riots in France this month, he accurately described them as student protests against poor conditions in public schools. But he also said that Trump “is blaming Islam and unchecked immigration” for the unrest. What the audience did not hear is that there is no basis whatsoever for the president’s claim. Is there not some obligation for the newsman to inform his viewers, I ask him, when one side of the story he’s relaying is false?
Baier says that he often does push back on false information from Republicans. In recent interviews, he pressed Trump on his past claim that the Iran war would be “fairly quick” and Bessent on the president’s dreadful approval ratings. He describes his role these days as that of a hockey goalie, blocking whatever bad information he can from reaching the back of the net. But the balance doctrine also creates an uncomfortable obligation to host Trump’s breathless defenders on Special Report.
Take the case of Mollie Hemingway, a pundit who once blasted Trump as a “demagogue” but now plays the part of Trump booster on Baier’s show, amplifying his conspiracy theories about elections and more. (She went so far as to write a book about the 2020 election called Rigged.) Is there any point at which Baier considers whether someone like Hemingway should continue to be on air? He pauses for a while.
“I’m still the goalie,” he says. “If Mollie said something that was egregious on the panel, I would step in and confront. But to hear where the Trump administration stands or what they’re thinking, I think is actually valuable in the discussion.” Special Report often pairs these pro-Trump voices with liberal pundits like Jessica Tarlov and Leslie Marshall, and its Common Ground segment brings together lawmakers from both sides of the aisle.
But the view that Trump’s side should be thoroughly represented shapes much of what airs on Special Report. That might come down to earnest belief, or survival instinct. (The newsmen who faced the wrath of the Fox audience after expressing too much skepticism of Trump could fill Cafe Milano.) “I think history will judge whether he’s been, in the big picture, this great figure or whether he has been what some would describe as a divisive figure,” Baier says. “But Donald Trump will be a consequential president in history’s mind. And how you read it will be what point of view you come from.”
One wonders how Baier would judge the history we’re living through. He’s written nine books, all New York Times bestsellers, including six about American presidents. His latest, The Case for America, is a paean to the founding ideals of the country. In the introduction, Baier outlines several “bedrock principles” that defined the founding of the United States: freedom of speech, freedom of the press, freedom of religion, and the peaceful transfer of power. I point out that Trump in many ways represents the antithesis of those principles—between the 2020 election crisis, his attempted “Muslim ban,” his crackdown on the press, the legal harassment of his critics… There’s too much to list over a two-course dinner. Did that come to mind as he was writing the book?
“It wasn’t specifically written like that,” Baier says. “But it was specific to look back at what’s important to the founders and what they believe. So if you take that away from that, that’s fine.” He adds: “I think there are a lot of Trump people who would push back at some of your characterizations about lack of freedom for religion.”
Did Trump not run on banning Muslims from the United States?
“It didn’t last long,” Baier says, apparently reassured by the judicial limitations placed on Trump’s crusade. I ask about the threats to the American project that his book warns against—extremism, venality, hyperpartisan coarseness. Is Trump not the primary culprit driving those trends? The day prior, I point out, the president called Annie Andrews, the Democratic US Senate candidate in South Carolina, “Trannie Andrews.”
Baier pauses. “Some of the rhetoric is quite something,” he says. “But it’s all part of the story. Clearly, Donald Trump hasn’t done the ‘common ground’ part of my book as well as anybody else. But he got elected by the population in this country, and so he’s the president of the United States.”
What does that afford him? A pass on some of this?
“Not a pass. We definitely have to cover it and have on the critics of how he operates, but also listen to the administration’s side, because what Donald Trump says is one thing, and things that he does are another thing.”
Earlier that evening, as a black car carries us from the Fox bureau to Milano, Baier is reminiscing about his long career in Washington. We pass the Kennedy Center, an institution he once frequented as a crystal-clinking veteran of the capital’s cocktail party circuit, and I ask what he makes of Trump’s hostile takeover and subsequent destruction of the arts center.
He pauses. “It’s a fascinating story,” he says.
I try again. The scaffolding hiding Trump’s foiled attempt to add his name to the memorial is interesting, isn’t it?
“It’s a fascinating story,” he says again.
news.summary: On a night out at his “clubhouse” in Washington, the Fox News anchor weighs in on Trump’s war with the media, his old colleague Pete Hegseth, and how history will judge our increasingly wild national climate.

Did he stutter?

Who knew a reality show could end the greatest nation on earth?

news.title: NAACP Announces Massive Nationwide Campaign to Mobilize Black Male Voters
news.text:
With the upcoming midterm elections holding immense consequences, the power of the Black vote has never been more crucial. In an effort to mobilize communities across the country, the NAACP has announced a nationwide Week of Action from October 19 to October 24, leading up to the first-ever National Black Man Voter Day on Saturday, October 24, 2026.

​The campaign follows five weeks of national organizing calls that engaged thousands of Black men alongside a coalition of leading civil rights, civic engagement, and community organizations.

The initiative aims to mobilize 100,000 Black voters through coordinated civic engagement, community conversations, and group voting events where early voting is available—driven by local organizers, faith leaders, fraternity members, and student leaders.

Starting Monday, October 19, organizers will host community events focused on five pillars of Black men’s well-being: mental, physical, spiritual, financial, and civic health. Programming includes barbershop talks, wellness gatherings, faith-based events, financial discussions, and voter organizing.

RELATED: As Democrats Rise in the Polls, Black Voters Ask What’s in It for Them

Capping off the initiative on Saturday, October 24, National Black Man Voter Day will rally voters through rides, caravans, and campus events in early-voting states, while providing absentee and Election Day guidance everywhere else.

Derrick Johnson, NAACP President and CEO, spoke about bringing awareness to what is at stake in the upcoming election.

​”This midterm election is a critical turning point for our community and our democracy,” said Johnson in an official press release. “For many generations, Black men have fought to secure access to the ballot. Today, we wield our collective power and make our voices heard from the bottom of the ballot to the top. National Black Man Voter Day is about more than an election–this is about protecting our future and refusing to ever be silenced.”

Reflecting the shared vision of civil rights leaders across the country, Marc H. Morial, National Urban League President and CEO, shared how the movement emphasizes long-term community impact.

“When Black men vote, we are not simply casting ballots. We are claiming our power to shape the future of our families, our communities, and our nation,” he said. “National Black Man Voter Day is about turning that power into action. We are calling on Black men across America to make a plan, bring a brother with them, and show up in force. Our voices matter, our votes matter, and when we move together, we can move this nation forward.”

​To ensure a massive voter turnout, the coalition is co-led by the National Urban League, 100 Black Men of America, Black Men Vote, Woke Vote, and the NAACP has built a nationwide grassroots infrastructure. Other organizations such as Black Voters Matter, the National Pan-Hellenic Council, Until Freedom, the National Action Network, and State of the People have come out in support of the initiative.

​In 2024, Black men continued to vote Democratic at high rates—with nearly 80% backing Kamala Harris—even as Donald Trump captured about 21% of their vote, according to the Pew Research Center. With factors such as rising costs and economic anxiety, many Black men ultimately weighed inflation heavily when deciding whether to back Trump or stay undecided.

​Even with recent GOP gains, Black men still vote Democratic at higher rates than virtually any other major demographic group—surpassed only by Black women.

For information, visit www.blackmanvoterday.org.
news.summary:
A nationwide coalition of civil rights organizations is rallying thousands of Black men for a week, leading up to the inaugural National Black Man Voter Day.

He said a president seeking re-election should be prepared to meet voters and account for his performance, rather than rely on official engagements as a reason to avoid nationwide campaigning.

“What President Tinubu has done is a clear act of contempt against the Nigerian people. The APC is known for its contempt for Nigerians. He rejected the argument that official duties could prevent Tinubu from campaigning nationwide, citing former presidents Olusegun Obasanjo, Goodluck Jonathan and Muhammadu Buhari, as well as American presidential candidates Donald Trump and Kamala Harris.

“Saying that he (Tinubu) will be attending to official assignments is untrue, fake, deceitful and insincere. Didn’t former Presidents Olusegun Obasanjo, Goodluck Jonathan and Muhammadu Buhari attend to official duties while campaigning for their return tickets? Didn’t Donald Trump campaign? Didn’t Kamala Harris campaign? Why is Tinubu’s case different?” he queried.

He knows Nigerians are hungry and angry. He knows that the average Nigerian finds it difficult to eat and to be secure. He has failed on all fronts, so he is afraid to face Nigerians. He is running away from the reality he created,” he said.

He urged young Nigerians to reject the APC in 2027, warning that another term for the ruling party would prolong the hardship citizens were experiencing.

“I appeal to every young Nigerian to reject them. Let us collectively reject hunger, reject poverty, reject hardship and reject insecurity. The APC has brought only pain to Nigerians. It is time to say enough is enough,” he said.

Ologbondiyan described Atiku as physically fit and mentally alert, saying the former vice-president was prepared to campaign across the 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory. 

He pledged that an ADC government would pursue economic recovery, wealth creation, improved security and better living standards.

Douglas finally spoke up, noting that these reasons account for why Rogan rejected the Democrats in 2024. He then asked where Rogan stands now.

news.title: Kamala Harris Pitches Supreme Court, Electoral College Reform
news.text: Former Vice President Kamala Harris called for expanding the Supreme Court and changing the Electoral College during an interview with Keke Palmer, arguing that Democrats should pursue structural reforms if they regain control of Congress. “I believe that we need to expand the Supreme Court,” Harris said on the Baby, This is Keke Palmer podcast. “We need more justices on the Supreme Court so that we can have a court that actually reinforces the spirit and principles behind the Constitution of the United States.” Calls to expand the court, as well as term limits for justices, have come primarily from some Democrats, particularly after Republicans confirmed three justices during President Donald Trump's first term—Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh, and Amy Coney Barrett—giving conservatives a 6-3 majority that has since issued major rulings on abortion, voting rights, presidential power and other issues. Trump recently used this issue as a warning to Republicans, arguing that the GOP should act first or risk losing future elections. "The Dumocrats are openly stating that they plan to...EXPAND THE SUPREME COURT," he wrote in a Truth Social post in July, four months before the midterms, linking to a Politico article, which details a resolution from the Black, Hispanic and progressive caucus chairs that includes “enacting structural changes” to the court as well as other reforms. In the podcast episode released on Tuesday, Harris also said the popular vote “has to matter” and backed pushing for statehood for Washington, D.C., and Puerto Rico if their residents want it. Harris did not outline a specific plan for changing the presidential election system. Her remarks raised two distinct possibilities: replacing the Electoral College with a nationwide popular vote, and granting statehood to D.C. and Puerto Rico. Statehood would change their representation and electoral votes; by itself, it would not make the national popular vote determine the presidency. Newsweek has reached out to the Office of Kamala Harris outside of regular office hours for comment. What Expanding the Supreme Court Could Change The Constitution does not fix the Court’s size, so expansion could be done through legislation. Congress has changed the court's size several times throughout U.S. history, though the Supreme Court has had nine justices since 1869. Any newly created seats would be filled by presidential nomination and Senate confirmation. This means the political effect would depend on who controls the White House and Senate when seats are created and filled. More justices could shift the Court’s balance under a Democratic president, or a Republican one, and a future administration could seek to expand the Court again. A September Marquette Law School poll found that 53 percent of adults favored increasing the number of justices, while 47 percent opposed it. Support was sharply divided by party: 68 percent of Democrats favored expansion, compared with 35 percent of Republicans; 56 percent of independents were in favor. Popular Vote Has Majority Support but a Partisan Divide Under the current system, states appoint electors, and most award all their electoral votes to the statewide winner. That allows a presidential candidate to win the Electoral College without winning the most votes nationwide. A direct popular vote would make the national vote total decisive. A 2024 Pew Research Center survey found that 63 percent of Americans preferred changing the system so the candidate with the most votes nationally wins, while 35 percent favored keeping the Electoral College. Eight in 10 Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents supported replacing it; Republicans were more divided, with 53 percent favoring the current system and 46 percent preferring a popular vote. The proposal is often viewed as more favorable to Democrats, who won the national popular vote in seven of the eight presidential elections from 1992 through 2020. But that is no guarantee of future outcomes: Donald Trump won both the popular vote and Electoral College in 2024. A constitutional amendment replacing the Electoral College would need two-thirds support in both chambers of Congress and ratification by three-quarters of the states. Another approach, the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, would direct participating states’ electors to the national popular-vote winner once states totaling at least 270 electoral votes have joined. Harris Has Not Decided on a 2028 Run Asked directly by Palmer whether she would run for president again, Harris replied: “I haven’t decided. I haven’t decided yet. I will, I promise.” She said her focus was on the 2026 midterms, adding: “’28 don’t matter if we don’t do ’26 right.” Harris is leading early Democratic primary polling. The latest RealClearPolling's average, through October 6, put her at 26.4 percent, ahead of California Governor Gavin Newsom at 14.4 percent. A Financial Times/Focaldata poll conducted October 3–6 had Harris at 30 percent and Newsom at 15 percent. Prediction markets tell a different story. Polymarket figures as of early Friday morning put Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez from New York at 17 percent, Newsom at 15 percent, Senator Jon Ossoff from Georgia at 14 percent and Harris at 7 percent to win the Democratic nomination. Those market prices are not polling, and no major Democratic candidate has declared a campaign.

In the world of “South Park” ― where every episode of the NSFW cartoon is designed to shock, offend or provoke ― nothing and no one is off-limits. Not celebrities, not religious figures and certainly not politicians.

But few have been skewered as relentlessly as President Donald Trump.

“South Park” has a long history of poking fun at the president, one that began well before the show turned its attention to the chaos of his administration.

Before Trump became a recurring target in his own right, the series introduced a Trump-inspired version of Mr. Garrison, the schoolteacher-turned-presidential candidate, during Season 19 in 2015. After Trump rose to political prominence that year, Garrison took on an increasingly Trump-like persona, serving as the show’s stand-in for several seasons before being phased out after Season 26 in 2023.

But in his second term, Trump has once again become a regular target of “South Park’s” scathing humor, as the show takes aim at his leadership through relentless mockery and countless below-the-belt jokes (literally).

“South Park” hasn’t always focused on America’s political landscape. Since its 1997 debut, the animated provocateur — which typically follows the outrageous misadventures of elementary school friends Stan, Kyle, Cartman and Kenny in their small Colorado town — has made a name for itself with crude, violent and grotesque dark comedy.

Over the years, creators Trey Parker and Matt Stone have turned virtually everyone and everything in pop culture, and well beyond, into fodder for their unapologetic satire. Although the duo opted to skip the 2024 presidential election between Trump and then-Vice President Kamala Harris, telling Vanity Fair they were tired of making fun of the former, his return to the White House has seemingly given the foul-mouthed satirists plenty of fresh material to work with.

“South Park” returned with even more pointed jabs at the Trump administration.

When “South Park” returned for Seasons 27 and 28 last year, Trump quickly found himself back in the show’s crosshairs. No aspect of his presidency seemed off-limits, from his administration’s immigration crackdown and push to bring religion into public schools to his penchant for litigation. That included his $16 million settlement with Paramount Global, the parent company of “South Park,” over edits to a “60 Minutes” interview with Harris.

The dispute even made its way into the Season 27 premiere, in which Trump sues the town of South Park after residents object to Jesus Christ’s presence at the local elementary school.

“You guys saw what happened to CBS? Yeah, well, guess who owns CBS? Paramount,” Jesus Christ says in the episode’s climax. “Do you really want to end up like Colbert?”

The latter line refers to former “Late Show” host Stephen Colbert, whose long-running CBS program was abruptly canceled last summer, shortly after he called Paramount’s settlement with Trump a “big fat bribe.”

Other Trump critics have also faced repercussions for challenging the president’s administration. For instance, late-night host Jimmy Kimmel, who has feuded with Trump for over a decade, said the president’s Federal Communications Commission repeatedly made threats last year over plans to interview Democratic state Rep. James Talarico on his show. The interview was ultimately moved to YouTube.

Kimmel also came close to suffering the same fate as Colbert, when ABC temporarily took his show off the air last year over remarks it described as “offensive and insensitive” regarding the assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk. In reality, Kimmel had condemned the killing while accusing MAGA supporters of “desperately trying to characterize this kid who murdered Charlie Kirk as anything other than one of them and doing everything they can to score political points from it.”

Meanwhile, “South Park” has somehow managed to avoid the same circumstances, as it continues to take on Trump with little consequence.

“South Park” doubled down on trolling Trump, even after the White House condemned it.

One possible reason for the show’s staying power is the $1.5 billion streaming deal creators Parker and Stone struck with Paramount just hours before “South Park” went scorched-earth on Trump last summer. The agreement not only cemented the series as one of television’s most valuable franchises, but also secured its future on Paramount’s Comedy Central through 2030, leaving plenty of room for more Trump takedowns in the years ahead.

The show’s massive audience, which includes a key segment of Trump’s base — young, white men — could also make it harder for the president to retaliate without alienating some of the very people he hopes to win over.

Still, that didn’t stop the White House from bashing “South Park” upon its return last year for mercilessly mocking Trump with small-penis jokes and depicting him in bed with Satan in the Season 27 premiere.

“This show hasn’t been relevant for over 20 years and is hanging on by a thread with uninspired ideas in a desperate attempt for attention. President Trump has delivered on more promises in just six months than any other president in our country’s history — and no fourth-rate show can derail President Trump’s hot streak,” the White House said in a statement to Rolling Stone. 

The criticism did little to slow the show’s momentum, however, as the Trump jokes continued throughout the rest of the season and even this year.

Ahead of the Sept. 16 premiere of Season 29, “South Park” jokingly announced it was changing its name to “South America,” a move “inspired by the bravery and patriotism of Apple and Google,” Parker and Stone said. The joke clearly referenced Trump’s recent renaming of Lake Ontario as “Lake America” and the tech giants that bowed to his decision.

The show’s creators also took another swipe at their parent company, Paramount, ending their announcement with a thank-you to “a Skydance Capitulation” — a dig at the company’s efforts to pander to the Trump administration last year to secure approval for its merger.

Neither jab drew a response from Trump or the White House this time. Not even the show’s opening gag, which features a naked Trump flossing his “teeny tiny” penis with the U.S. flag.

Jokes about the president and his administration have since cooled off, but any new controversy or antics could still make their way into a “South Park” episode, one way or another.

At an Emmy For Your Consideration event in May, Parker and Stone revealed they had originally planned to devote just one episode to Trump last year. But the administration’s swift pushback prompted them to double down and take their satire even further.

“We laid into him so hard, and the thing became: ‘Well, who’s the bully now?’” Parker said, per The Hollywood Reporter. “It became this just totally juvenile joke of like, ‘We’re not gonna stop. We’re going to do it every single week.’”

Backlash from MAGA supporters and others urging the creators to “move on” from Trump jokes only seemed to fuel them even more. As Parker explained, “To me, that was the whole season, was that they kept reacting, and we were like, ‘Well, God damn it. All right, we’ll do it some more.’”

Even if “South Park” eventually pulls back from its Trump focus, its continued on-air run has already shown a resilience many of the president’s detractors have struggled to match amid his administration’s attacks. That defiance, however, comes as little surprise from Parker and Stone, who have long refused to play it safe with their boundary-pushing comedy.

“It was a bully mentality,” Stone said at their FYC event, adding that the duo would rather lose everything than compromise their creative freedom. “We don’t care. We don’t give a fuck. We say it all the time. We’re not irresponsible, but we’ll go back to Colorado. We don’t give a fuck.”
news.author: Njera Perkins

news.title: Harry Enten Flags New Fox News Poll Detail That Could Seriously Unsettle Trump
news.text:
CNN chief data analyst Harry Enten on Thursday highlighted new Fox News polling showing what he described as an “absolutely stunning” collapse in support for Donald Trump among voters under 30.

“They no longer think that Trump is groovy. He’s no longer jiggy with it,” Enten teed up his analysis, noting that Trump’s net approval rating among younger voters has fallen from +3 percentage points in October 2024 to -50 now, according to the poll.

“This is math we can all do,” said Enten. “53 points in the wrong direction amongst a group he was once positive with. It’s absolutely stunning.”

Trump’s performance on the economy and inflation appears to be driving much of the decline, Enten argued.

During the 2024 presidential election campaign, voters under 30 favored Trump over his Democratic rival Kamala Harris by 2 percentage points on the economy, he noted. But Trump’s net approval rating among the same age group on the issue now stands at -64 percentage points.

Enten also highlighted what he called Trump’s “eye-popping” numbers on inflation, with just 9% of younger voters approving of his handling of the issue and 91% disapproving.

“There are more Americans who think that we faked the moon landing than the percentage of young voters who actually approve of the job that Trump is doing on inflation,” said Enten. “These numbers are some of the worst I have ever seen in any poll, on any issue for any president.”
news.author: Lee Moran

news.title: 2027: Tinubu Afraid to Face Nigerians, Has No Business Seeking Re-election — ADC Campaign Council
news.text:
The African Democratic Congress Presidential Campaign Council (ADC-PCC) has accused President Bola Tinubu of avoiding Nigerians ahead of the 2027 presidential election, arguing that his reported decision not to campaign across all 36 states shows contempt for the electorate.

The council claimed that the development could benefit its presidential candidate, Atiku Abubakar, insisting that Nigerians deserve a leader who is willing to defend his record, answer questions and explain his plans for the country.

The ADC-PCC Director of Media and Publicity, Kola Ologbondiyan, made the remarks while receiving a delegation of youths under the platform of Young Voters for Atiku (YVA).

Ologbondiyan maintained that any president seeking re-election should be ready to engage voters nationwide and account for his performance, rather than cite official responsibilities as a reason to avoid campaigning across the country.

“What President Tinubu has done is a clear act of contempt against the Nigerian people. The APC is known for its contempt for Nigerians. How can a man who wants to be re-elected as president, after failing woefully, say he does not want to visit the people he seeks to govern? It is an aberration of norm,” he said.

He dismissed the argument that official duties could prevent Tinubu from embarking on a nationwide campaign, pointing to former Nigerian presidents Olusegun Obasanjo, Goodluck Jonathan and Muhammadu Buhari, as well as American presidential candidates Donald Trump and Kamala Harris, as examples of political leaders who campaigned while pursuing or seeking to retain office.

“Saying that he (Tinubu) will be attending to official assignments is untrue, fake, deceitful and insincere. Didn’t former Presidents Olusegun Obasanjo, Goodluck Jonathan and Muhammadu Buhari attend to official duties while campaigning for their return tickets? Didn’t Donald Trump campaign? Didn’t Kamala Harris campaign? Why is Tinubu’s case different?” Ologbondiyan queried.

The ADC spokesperson further alleged that widespread public dissatisfaction over hunger, poverty, insecurity and economic hardship was responsible for Tinubu’s reported reluctance to meet voters across the country.

“He knows Nigerians are hungry and angry. He knows that the average Nigerian finds it difficult to eat and to be secure. He has failed on all fronts, so he is afraid to face Nigerians. He is running away from the reality he created,” he said.

Ologbondiyan called on young Nigerians to reject the All Progressives Congress (APC) in the 2027 elections, arguing that another term for the ruling party would prolong the hardship citizens are experiencing.

“I appeal to every young Nigerian to reject them. Let us collectively reject hunger, reject poverty, reject hardship and reject insecurity. The APC has brought only pain to Nigerians. It is time to say enough is enough,” he said.

He also described Atiku as physically fit and mentally alert, claiming that the former vice-president was prepared to campaign across all 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory.

According to Ologbondiyan, an ADC-led government would prioritise economic recovery, wealth creation, improved security and better living standards.

“Atiku Abubakar will bring back subsidy to reduce cost of petroleum products, create wealth, end hunger in our land, secure our nation and restore our battered economy. He has the experience, the capacity and the compassion to rescue Nigeria. He is fit, ready and prepared to lead Nigeria out of this present predicament,” Ologbondiyan added.

The ADC-PCC also claimed that the inauguration of the APC Presidential Campaign Council had strengthened its political position, alleging that no ADC members or sympathisers endorsed the event.

news.title: America's Reddest State is No Longer Considered Safe For Republicans
news.text: America’s most Republican state is no longer considered entirely safe for the GOP in the race for its sole House seat, according to a leading election forecaster. Inside Elections moved Wyoming’s at-large congressional district from “Solid Republican” to “Likely Republican” in its latest House ratings, published Thursday. The change means a Republican defeat would still be a major upset, but the seat is no longer in the forecaster’s most secure category. The downgrade is remarkable given Wyoming’s recent voting history. President Donald Trump won 71.6 percent of the state’s vote in the 2024 presidential election, compared with 25.84 percent for Kamala Harris. Wyoming’s official results recorded 192,633 votes for Trump and 69,527 for Harris. Trump's 45.76-point victory was his largest margin in any state, while his vote share was the highest recorded by a presidential nominee in Wyoming, surpassing Ronald Reagan’s 70.51 percent in 1984. “The most Republican state in the country shouldn’t be anywhere close to the House battleground,” Inside Elections' Jacob Rubashkin and Inshara Ali wrote in the forecaster's October 15 update. “But Trump is barely above water according to private polling, and GOP nominee Chuck Gray, the state secretary of state, is deeply unpopular statewide.” Gray won a crowded Republican primary with 31,224 votes, or 25.3 percent, finishing five points ahead of his nearest rival. Democratic nominee Lisa Kinney, a lawyer and former state senator, won her primary with 9,344 votes, or 76.5 percent. However, Kinney entered the campaign with limited resources. Federal Election Commission records show her campaign raised $17,946 and held $2,009.75 in cash as of July 29. The seat is open because Republican Representative Harriet Hageman is running for the Senate. Libertarian Shawn Johnson and Constitution Party candidate Jeff Haggit are also on the November 3 ballot. Inside Elections said Gray’s “unique vulnerabilities” could produce Wyoming’s closest House contest since Democrat Gary Trauner narrowly lost in 2006 and 2008. Other forecasters continue to place the contest firmly in the Republican column, meaning the rating change is not evidence that Democrats are favored to win. It does, however, suggest that candidate-specific concerns and Trump’s standing may have made an extraordinarily Republican state less predictable than its recent election results would indicate. This is a developing story. More to follow. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here.
news.summary: “The most Republican state” is near the House battleground as Trump and GOP nominee Chuck Gray struggle, a forecaster says.
news.author: Sam Stevenson

news.title: Trump Voter Who Called Him 'Big Daddy Trump' Says He Is Being Crushed by Insurance and Gas Prices
news.text: A Donald Trump voter who once feared the prospect of Kamala Harris winning the White House says he is struggling with health insurance costs and rising gas prices, expressing frustration with the president he trusted ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.John, from Pennsylvania, told SiriusXM's The Megyn Kelly Wrap-Up Show that his family was struggling to make ends meet despite his support for Trump in the 2024 election. Speaking to host Emily Jashinsky, he said he was 'angry' with the president, whom he still calls 'Big Daddy Trump'.'I'm self-employed. My insurance, my health insurance, has turned into, now, like a huge mortgage payment with a huge deductible,' John said, describing the added expense of insuring his two teenage sons, who had recently started driving, before turning to another source of frustration. 'Gas prices are insane,' he said.'I Trusted Trump 1,000%'John said he backed Trump because he was 'horrified at the thought' of former Vice President Kamala Harris winning the 2024 presidential election. However, the financial pressures he described have left him questioning that support.'But I got to tell you, I'm angry,' he said. 'I trusted Trump,' he added, explaining that he had supported the president completely and 'trusted him 1,000%.' John said he had worried about the cost of insurance before the election but now felt he was 'getting clobbered' by rising expenses. 'My wife also, she's self-employed. We're struggling,' he said, describing insurance costs as a major concern.'John stopped short of saying he had switched political allegiance, telling Jashinsky that he was 'up in the air right now.' He also expressed reservations about the political alternatives, criticising what he described as 'blue-haired liberals and this weird nonsense.'Despite those reservations, John said he was unhappy with how things had turned out. 'I don't want to say lied to, but I'm upset,' he said.Fox News Poll Shows Sharp Drop in ApprovalJohn's concerns come as a Fox News poll found Trump's overall job approval had fallen to its lowest level in the network's polling during either of his presidential terms. The poll, conducted from 9 to 12 October among 1,202 registered voters, found that 36% approved of Trump's performance as president, while 64% disapproved. The margin of error was 2.5 percentage points.Trump's handling of inflation received even less support. Just 22% of respondents approved of his performance on the issue, down from 36% in a survey conducted last summer, according to Fox News.The decline was particularly pronounced among voters under 45, those with annual household incomes below $50,000, non-white voters, and people without a college degree, according to the outlet. The findings come as the administration faces scrutiny over the cost of living, an issue that featured prominently in Trump's 2024 campaign.Iran War Adds Pressure on Fuel CostsThe war with Iran has also added to pressure on US energy prices, with rising fuel costs becoming a concern for voters ahead of the midterm elections. At a 16 September rally in Gastonia, North Carolina, Trump described higher gas prices as 'a very inexpensive price to pay for what we've done' and predicted they would fall.'But that's going to come tumbling down,' Trump said of gas prices. 'That's going to be like rocket ships in reverse.'For voters such as John, however, the immediate concern is whether his family's household expenses will become more manageable. His account highlights the gap between his earlier confidence in Trump and his current frustration over the costs confronting his family.
news.author: Regyl Jaen

news.title: Sexual harassment scandal shapes southwest suburban Illinois House race
news.text:
A far southwest suburban statehouse election race offers a rare instance of a competitive Chicago-area district on Illinois’ heavily gerrymandered legislative map.

But the 97th House contest has been driven largely by a subject all too common in Springfield: sexual harassment.

Republican Gabby Shanahan is out to win the seat she fell short of two years ago to disgraced ex-state Rep. Harry Benton, the Plainfield Democrat who stepped down this summer amid allegations of making lewd comments to three women.

State Rep. Jessica Dixon Heitman is seeking a full term after Will and Kendall County Democratic Party leaders appointed her in July to replace Benton — whose alleged misbehavior raised “red flags” during her own brief 2023 stint as a contracted media relations consultant in his office, the new lawmaker has said.

Shanahan and her campaign have accused Dixon Heitman of “staying silent” on Benton’s conduct toward a young staffer who later described a litany of disturbing interactions with the ex-lawmaker. A former legislative inspector general determined Benton’s behavior broke state law.

Dixon Heitman told the Farmers Weekly Review of Will County that she respected the wishes of the young complainant who “was very opposed to filing any sort of report.” The lawmaker also told The Illinoize she “was personally affected by Rep. Benton’s behavior.”

Illinois Republicans are trying to make the same case statewide against House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch, who is facing criticism from within his own Democratic caucus for directing $1.4 million to Benton’s 2024 reelection campaign.

And it’s a recurring theme in the Capitol, where ex-Speaker Michael Madigan ceded the gavel to Welch in 2021 after a downfall precipitated in part by Madigan’s mishandling of harassment allegations in his 13th Ward political organization.

Welch maintains that while his office was aware of alleged misconduct, he had no choice but to continue backing Benton without a formal complaint to spur an investigation. The speaker booted Benton from the caucus this February when another woman filed a complaint.

Benton has denied wrongdoing — and hasn’t given up his elected post as Wheatland Township highway commissioner.

Shanahan, who lost to Benton by about four percentage points in 2024, argues that “had something been said three years ago, two more victims or survivors would not have been in that situation.”

As a court-appointed special advocate for children in the Kendall County court system, Shanahan is legally mandated to report instances of potential harassment.

“I have a 24-year-old daughter, and if something like that happened to her and nobody advocated for her, I’d have a problem with it,” said Shanahan, a Joliet resident. “If you see something, you should say something… The culture perpetuates when we continue to allow it to happen.”

Dixon Heitman declined interview requests, responding via email to a Sun-Times reporter only after a spokesman from Welch’s office called to ask what sort of questions she’d be asked.

“At the end of the day, I believe this race is about accountability and delivering for the people I represent,” she wrote. “I’m running to build a future where working families can afford to thrive, seniors can retire with dignity, and every child has the opportunity to succeed.”

Moderate stances in a purple district

Dixon Heitman, a granddaughter of the late former U.S. Sen. Alan Dixon, formerly worked as a statehouse media relations staffer before helming her own PR firm.

The Plainfield resident wrote that “as a working mom raising three daughters, I understand how difficult it can be to balance the costs of raising a family today while also planning for the future. That’s why I’ve focused my efforts on lowering healthcare costs, protecting critical services that seniors rely on, expanding opportunities for good-paying jobs, and making sure people can retire with dignity and security.”

Shanahan agreed the top issue for constituents in their purple district is lowering the cost of living, especially property taxes. “Because of Springfield politicians, your gas is taxed twice and you have the second highest gas tax in the nation, on top of your highest property taxes in the nation,” she said.

Both candidates mostly steer clear of more polarizing political bellwethers in their purple district, where voters supported Kamala Harris by about 4% over President Donald Trump in 2024.

Dixon Heitman’s campaign doesn’t outwardly attack Trump administration policies as aggressively as other Illinois House Democrats, while Shanahan declined to say specifically if she voted for Trump.

“He’s going to do what he’s going to do… I supported the Republican Party in 2024,” said Shanahan, who also declined to share her personal stance on abortion rights.

“It’s already settled in the state of Illinois, so I don’t think it’s a legislative issue,” she said.

Dixon Heitman supports a state constitutional amendment codifying abortion rights, and she carried a financial advantage into the home stretch of the race. 

She entered October with about $79,000 in her campaign fund and reported in-kind contributions totaling more than $200,000, the vast majority provided by the Welch-controlled Democrats for the Illinois House committee.

Shanahan’s campaign entered October with almost $48,000 on hand, reporting $141,000 worth of in-kind contributions, mostly courtesy of the House Republican Organization.
news.author: Mitchell Armentrout

news.title: Black homeownership should be a GOP selling point, not a HUD target
news.text:
Guy Benson made the same case about energy in these pages this month: Republicans, starting with the president, should have been “consistently seeding the message.” With black voters, the message is sitting in plain sight.

That message is ownership: property and capital in private hands, not dependence on government. Republicans have a claim to it that goes back to President Richard Nixon, who created the federal minority business office in 1969. Former President George W. Bush set a goal of 5.5 million new minority homeowners. Trump’s own 2020 Platinum Plan promised to advance homeownership in black communities, and Wells Fargo made its $60 billion pledge in his first year in office.

Candidates have numbers to work with. Black household income rose 4.8% last year after falling 3.3% in 2024. Black homeownership was 45.4% this spring, up from 43.9% a year earlier, and the black Conservative Federation’s new report sets a goal of a 5-point gain within a decade.

Not every number flatters. Black unemployment rose to 7% in September, a statistically significant jump. Good or bad, numbers like these are how Washington measures progress. It rarely writes black-only policy, whatever the loudest voices on either side claim. It keeps score, as former President Barack Obama’s White House did in 2016, crediting work to improve the lives of “all Americans, including African Americans.”

In Trump’s first term, the message had authors. Ja’Ron Smith, a domestic policy aide who worked closely with Jared Kushner, got credit for opportunity zones, criminal justice reform and funding for historically black colleges and universities. Turner ran the opportunity zone council, which ended in 2020 and was never restored. Last year, the president ordered Nixon’s minority business agency cut to the legal minimum.

Candidates cannot deliver a message the administration has not articulated.

What it has conveyed is opposition. Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon, the Justice Department’s civil rights chief, has described past enforcement as a form of “benevolent racism.” She has a point. Government should not sort citizens by race. But opposition alone tells black voters what Republicans are against. It does not tell them what Republicans offer.

Turner turned that opposition into an investigation. Equal treatment under the law is the right standard. So look at the law. Congress wrote special-purpose credit programs into the Equal Credit Opportunity Act in 1976, and President Gerald Ford signed it. Federal regulators encouraged lenders to create them in February 2022. That April, Wells Fargo announced one: $150 million to help minority homeowners refinance at lower rates, paid from its own lending division. This August, seven agencies led by HUD withdrew the guidance. HUD opened its inquiry six weeks later.

Washington wrote the law, encouraged the program and then investigated the bank that took it at its word.

Conservatives were right to fight quotas, but a private company spending its own capital is the market at work. If those programs offend equal treatment, change the rule or change the statute. No candidate can brag about black homeownership while Washington investigates a pledge to raise it.

Candidates are writing their own message instead. Rep. Byron Donalds (R-FL), one of three nominees who would be the first black Republican elected governor in their respective states, held a town hall at Florida A&M University, a historically black university in Tallahassee. Students pressed him on his loyalty to the GOP, and he turned the question back on the party they support. “You’ve been faithful to that party,” Donalds said. “Have they been faithful to you?”

It is the right question. He has also bought BET airtime for an ad touting his support for the school. Nobody calls that un-American. It’s called competing. But a candidate who asks whether Democrats delivered has to say what Republicans will deliver, and Washington is not helping him.

So why do so few black Republicans say this out loud? There are not many of us, and for us, access is the currency. Black Democrats make the same trade. Three weeks after then-President Joe Biden’s debate, just one of roughly 60 Congressional Black Caucus members had called for him to go. The caucus stood by him, and it did not save him. Then-Vice President Kamala Harris later won 83% of black voters, down from Biden’s 91%.

SPIKE IN MORTGAGE RATES COMPOUNDS INFLATION AND DEBT WOES

The path forward is short. Charge a violation or close the investigation. Restore the council. Adopt a number, such as the federation’s five-point homeownership goal, and reach it through sound credit, not loosened standards. Give every Republican candidate the same sentence to say in November and 2028.

Black Democrats’ loyalty did not save Biden. Our silence will not save this coalition.

Melik Abdul is a Washington-based public affairs professional, writer, and Republican strategist.
news.summary: On Oct. 7, Housing and Urban Development Secretary Scott Turner opened an investigation into Wells Fargo over its pledges to increase black homeownership. He said the bank’s conduct was “immoral, unethical and un-American” even if it broke no law. Raising black homeownership is a Republican goal, and a Republican administration is investigating a bank for […]
news.author: Melik Abdul

news.title: Trump’s Slurs Come Back to Bite New Mouthpiece
news.text:
President Donald Trump’s habit of belittling rivals who failed the bar exam has come back to haunt him as his new mouthpiece fends off questions about her legal credentials.

Trump’s new White House press secretary Katie Zacharia, whom the president introduced as “an attorney,” admitted Thursday that she failed California’s bar exam after graduating from law school in 2011.

Trump, 80, has repeatedly mocked his political rivals over their bar exam records, even calling then-Vice President Kamala Harris a “moron” in 2024, despite her having passed the exam on her second attempt in 1990.

Meanwhile, his administration has offered a more glowing assessment of Zacharia. White House Communications Director Steven Cheung described her as “uniquely qualified and whip smart” as questions mount over how the 41-year-old mother of four has presented her legal background.
