news.title: Jon Ossoff’s rise to US Senate was meteoric – how high can he go?
news.text:
Jon Ossoff has “zero interest” in running for president in 2028, he declared during a debate this week. Jon Ossoff has “zero interest” in running for president in 2028, he told a local TV station last month. Jon Ossoff has “zero interest” in running for president in 2028, he told MS Now – twice – in August.

The Democratic US senator for Georgia said as much to CNN. And the Atlanta Journal-Constitution. And MS Now, again. And in his second Senate debate on Tuesday night.

Are you getting the message?

Plenty aren’t. It doesn’t matter how many times the media-savvy senator delivers his well-rehearsed line: in Washington, and beyond, there is markedly more than “zero interest” in the prospect of Ossoff running for the White House.

His political rise in a Republican-leaning swing state, his viral speeches on conspicuously national issues, and Democratic demand for a new figure to lead the party forward are conspiring to fan the flames of speculation.

But when Ossoff, 39, lands on a message, he sticks to it like gum under a desk. His discipline and doggedness show up in Senate hearings, in campaign rallies and debates – railing against “the Epstein class” and mocking Trump in blunt snippets that spread far and wide online.

After Donald Trump won Georgia by two points in the 2024 presidential election, Ossoff had been expected to face one of the most bruising contests of any incumbent US senator this November. The race, however, does not appear close. Ossoff – whose team declined repeated requests for an interview for this story – has consistently led between four and eight points in most polls against his challenger, the Republican congressman Mike Collins – a lead no Democrat has posted in Georgia since the late 1990s.

On the debate stage in October, Ossoff hammered away at Collins, dubbing the encounter the “trial of Mike Collins”, and demanding Collins explain his votes in support of the Iran war and the president’s tariffs, as well as ties to white nationalists in his office and his family.

“If John Lewis were marching today from Selma to Montgomery, Mike Collins would be grabbing a billy club,” Ossoff declared. “His office has been in cahoots with some of the most notorious white supremacists in the country. He himself has amplified neo-Nazi propaganda. He’s never apologized for it. And he should tonight.”

Ossoff’s ability to deliver such lines – as memorable as they are clippable in this social media age – is part of his broader approach to winning support, vote by vote, in a state where it cannot be taken for granted.

“A campaign is just a bigger, longer jury trial,” said Charlie Bailey, director of the Georgia Democratic party, and a trial lawyer by trade. “The best trial lawyers, they are themselves. They talk plainly to the jury. They say straightforward things, and the jury can tell that they’re being themselves, and they just believe what they are saying.”

When Ossoff talks to voters, “it not only matches up with their experience, their anger, and their frustration; they know he’s telling the truth”, Bailey said. “That’s leadership.”

Ossoff has not always been a winner. His meteoric political rise dates back almost a decade, to a defeat.

When Republican Tom Price resigned his congressional seat in February 2017, after Trump appointed him to serve as health and human services secretary, Ossoff stepped into a special election with a “jungle” primary for Georgia’s sixth congressional district: the candidates of all parties run on a single ballot, with a runoff between the top two if no one wins more than 50% of the vote.

It looked like a stretch. “You have to remember, everyone on the local level was a Republican,” said John Ernst, former mayor of Brookhaven, a city in Atlanta’s northern suburbs; at the time, Ernst was the only Democratic mayor in the district.

The district was, in short, “the bastion of the proto-Maga movement”, said Ernst, “but without the craziness. It’s the business wing of the movement.”

But Atlanta’s streets had filled that year with women in pink hats in the largest such demonstration since the civil rights movement, and they were looking for a way to strike back.

This special congressional election provided stunned Democratic voters their first chance to register their outrage at Trump’s provocations, at least by proxy.

“There’s all this momentum, and there’s all these people excited, and things are going pretty crappy at the national level, and I probably then started to think, ‘Huh, this is interesting,’” Lynn Deutsch, mayor of Dunwoody, Georgia, said. Ossoff raised an eye-watering $23m in small donations from around the country.

While Ossoff took the former Georgia secretary of state Karen Handel to a runoff, Handel – a notably moderate Republican – beat Ossoff 52-48. But Ossoff walked away with the largest Democratic donor database in the US.

After his 2017 defeat, “everyone” was asking Ossoff the same thing, according to Ernst. It is a question he is likely to get just as much, if not more, should he meet expectations and win next month: what is he going to do next?

“Think about it. He was a guy who came out of the blue,” Ernst said. “He wasn’t a known entity outside of a few congressional offices in Washington DC.”

He didn’t completely come out of the blue, of course. Ossoff grew up in Northlake, then a middle-class unincorporated part of DeKalb county near Atlanta. His mother, Heather Fenton, is a prominent political figure in her own right, who co-founded New Power Pac, which worked to elect women to local offices in Georgia. His father, Richard Ossoff, was an attorney.

In his youth, Jon Ossoff took his parents’ political capital and an education at Atlanta’s elite Paideia school to an internship with Representative John Lewis before undergraduate study at Georgetown.

He later worked for Hank Johnson, a Democratic congressman who represents part of Atlanta and DeKalb county. Ossoff left to earn a master’s degree from the London School of Economics in 2013.

Using $250,000 of an inheritance to buy a stake in a documentary film company, Ossoff spent the next four years in London, producing investigations as the CEO of Insight TWI, covering corruption and human rights abuses, looking at Fifa, Beijing’s investments in Africa, and working on a documentary on female Yazidi soldiers, which aired on the BBC.

He returned home to run for Congress. And one defeat was not enough to kill his political aspirations. Following his 2017 loss, however, Ossoff decided against challenging Handel to a rematch in 2018. Instead, he started building political relationships across the state of Georgia, using his war chest and new national standing to help Democrats in local elections.

Ossoff campaign in 2017 sowed seeds that he subsequently spent years watering.

“When I ran in 2011 for the first time on council, I did it by myself. I had no idea what I was doing,” Deutsch said. “I ran for mayor [in 2019] but I wasn’t going to do it by myself. So I convened all these women … and they had all helped on the Jon campaign. And they had all knocked on doors for Ossoff.”

One by one, local offices began to flip. Dissent against the Trump administration from Atlanta’s professional class had crystallized into sustained, organized political action.

Three years after Ossoff’s loss, Democrats had taken control of local offices in most of Atlanta’s affluent, politically powerful northern suburbs. Many had been involved with Ossoff’s congressional campaign.

“There was just an energy about him,” Deutsch said of Ossoff, in the shadow of Trump’s first presidency. “And remember, everybody was operating kind of from a space of panic, right? What the heck just happened? And when you talk about the areas that flipped, they’re generally highly educated. We didn’t just flip because there were Democrats who weren’t voting. We flipped because there were people who were independents, mostly, that said, ‘I can’t vote for Republicans any more.’”

When Ossoff announced his campaign for US Senate in November 2019, no one knew what was on the horizon. The Covid-19 pandemic turned the race on its head, as he accused his opponent – the incumbent Republican senator David Perdue, one of the wealthiest lawmakers in US history – of corruption.

Perdue was the most active stock trader in the Senate, and made some opportune trades during the pandemic. Ossoff pounced, characterizing his opponent as a caricature of Gilded Age wealth.

“It’s not just that you’re a crook, senator. It’s that you’re attacking the health of the people that you represent,” Ossoff told Perdue during one debate. “You did say Covid-19 was no deadlier than the flu. You did say there would be no significant uptick in cases. All the while, you were looking after your own assets and your own portfolio. And you did vote four times to end protections for pre-existing conditions. Four times.”

Perdue pulled out of the final debate, as money poured into the race. Ossoff debated an empty podium to make his message heard.

Perdue raised about $100m to defend his seat. Ossoff raised more than $150m to challenge him.

But Georgia voters had heard enough. Ossoff beat Perdue by about 56,000 votes, 50.6% to 49.4%.

“Everybody who cast your ballot, everybody who put your faith and confidence in democracy’s capacity to deliver the representation we deserve, whether you were for me or against me, I’ll be for you,” he said in his victory speech.

Donald Chase is a peanut farmer from south Georgia. He lives 30 miles (48.2km) away from Plains, where Jimmy Carter rose from obscurity to the White House 50 years ago. There are few Carter Democrats left in south Georgia. But there are some Republicans voting for Ossoff; Chase is among them.

“He’s not afraid to stand up, and I appreciate that,” said Chase. “The second thing is he’s demonstrated really clearly that he’ll come to south Georgia, that he’ll listen to the issues, and he’ll try to do something where he can.”

“Republican leadership in Georgia has done a lot of good things,” added Chase. But tariffs and diesel fuel prices have damaged the peanut business.

“The tariff situation, I saw it coming, and I just was – this is going to hurt peanut farmers,” he said. “Our two primary export countries are Canada and Mexico. And with this latest spat, I will call it, the tariffs on peanut products went up 295%.”

Ossoff still faces the same challenge Democrats up and down the ballot face, two years after the party’s crushing defeat to Trump: motivating the base.

A young Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) worker, who requested anonymity for fear of political retribution, described life under the leadership of the health and human services secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr – a key Trump appointee – while watching Atlanta’s Pride parade this month.

“We’re personally very, very burnt out, and very overstretched,” she said. “We’re just nervous that we’re going to get fired every single day.”

She has knocked on doors for Ossoff in the past, and plans to vote for him. But that’s about it.

“I feel like I’ve done that a lot over the past few years, especially for Stacey Abrams and Kamala [Harris],” she said. “I think I’m just burnt out. I’m going to vote and I’m going to encourage people to vote, but I’m not doing what I’ve done in the past because it’s just been too much.”

At the same event Rockwell McKay said: “Even if his heart is in the right place and he’s trying to do these things, he can’t do it in two or four years.

“They churn up in the House with the Democrats and the Republicans. In the next three or four years, we’ll have somebody else in wanting to redirect their movement. I don’t see it.

“I’m past the Obama shit, with the hope,” he added. “Fuck all that.”

Ossoff is, in many ways, unique. Should he ever find himself drawn away from Georgia, Democrats in the state fear his successes would be hard to replicate – in part because he has a gift for being the right person, in the right place, at the right time.

Contributors have given him more than $98m for November’s election, with about 90% of donations under $100. Ossoff had about $43m as cash on hand at the end of July: the largest war chest of any US Senate candidate in this election cycle, and 20 times as much as Collins, his opponent.

“Eventually, Jon Ossoff maybe should run for president, but not anytime soon,” said Deutsch, the Dunwoody mayor, who took solace in the fact he had “not indicated that it’s on his short-term, or even medium-term, plan”.

As senator, he has pushed hard to end stock and cryptocurrency trading by members of Congress, their spouses and dependent children; campaigned for a constitutional amendment to eliminate corporate spending in elections; and investigated abuses and corruption in federal prisons.

His departure from the role “would be a terrible loss” for Georgia in the Senate, she added. “But one of my young adult children, who lives in Texas, wants him to run. He thinks he’s the only choice. And I’m like, I don’t think so.”

Ernst, the former Brookhaven mayor, can see the appeal of an Ossoff presidential bid. “I mean, in this day and age, being a Democrat, white, male – young, white male – it’s kind of rare,” he said, as the Senate generally skews older. “And no one says he’s a raging liberal. No one says he’s conservative. No one says he’s moderate. He’s just Jon Ossoff.”

Johnson, the congressman for whom he used to work, said: “I think Jon’s cultivation of support from small-dollar donors from across the country strengthens his ability to pursue policy goals that favor the common good, as opposed to policies that favor the wealthy and the well connected.”

Twice, in 2017 and 2020, Ossoff found himself at the center of America’s political attention. Both times, he capitalized on that attention – to the political benefit of Democrats, and the financial benefit of his future campaigns.

Might he do it a third time? The chances are greater than zero.

news.title: The Perils of Believing the Pollsters Every October
news.text:
Everyone absorbing the elitist media spin on the midterm elections cannot avoid the swirling symphony of doom for the Republicans. Conventional wisdom suggests a good night for Democrats, and that’s before you look at the president’s dreadful approval rating. Polls can be tricky: one can disapprove of Trump and still vote the Republican party line.

All this doom might be accurate -- or it might turn out like 2016. Hillary Clinton had a 98 percent chance of winning, they said. Then-CBS Evening News anchor Scott Pelley suppressed his delight as he claimed “Time is running out for Donald Trump…No candidate down this far, this late, has ever recovered.” Over on ABC, Jonathan Karl echoed: “Donald Trump is down 17 points among women. You do not get elected ... .if you are down 17 points among women.”

news.title: Funny, irreverent, cocky: Can Abdul El-Sayed win a vital senate seat in abandoned America?
news.text:
The last of the wasps are dive-bombing through the long line of people waiting outside St Michael’s Catholic Church in the Carriage Town neighbourhood of Flint. Like many parts of the city, the street is a little careworn but the early autumn Saturday is summery and dazzling in its primary colours. Large gatherings of people are unusual here and several cars slow down so their occupants can ask people what’s going on. 

“Abdul El-Sayed is speaking here,” people from the line call to them and the faces reflect a carousel of interest, or perplexion or indifference as they roll up the windows and zoom off through wide, empty streets.

The event captures the odd contradiction of the US midterm senate races in that it is both inescapable on social media and almost invisible on the street. Attendees to El-Sayed’s rally are given the precise address just the day before the rally begins. The venue is small, which means it will be full. The vast majority of people in Flint have no idea it is taking place but within hours, the town hall will be spliced and diced and repackaged on social media. 

El-Sayed has been wandering Michigan relentlessly with his “It Shouldn’t be This Hard” tour. After Flint, he would head to Saginaw, where Paul Simon famously hitchhiked, and where the trajectory of the city’s fortunes was inextricably linked to the rise and fall of American motorcar production.

But Flint residents take rightful pride in the fact that their city is where it all began and argue that Flint is the true motor city.

“If you go right down here on Water Street where I live, they have the Durant building,” Michele Kelly explains, and talks me through the evolution of Charles Wisner and the “buzz car” and William Durant and the birth of General Motors. Kelly is 67 and has lived in Flint all her life. She’s fizzing with energy and is terrific fun, opening the conversation with a warning that New York mayor Zohran Mamdani is schooling the political classes on both sides on how to get it done. 

You think he’s that good, I ask?

“There’s no ‘think’ about it,” she clarifies.

When El-Sayed takes to the lectern in the church, the crowd waves placards and cheer as the candidate takes them through a now-familiar address that franks his love of Michigan, and his intentions for major reforms if he wins this senate race. 

His ascension to this moment has involved an epic uphill climb, first against the Democratic Party machine, whose favoured candidate, representative Haley Stevens, had the backing of the elders and the funding, outspending El-Sayed’s campaign by ten to one. That election illuminated the internal party chasm between the traditional ideological block of the party and the insurgent socialist democratic left. (El-Sayed has sought to position himself as a capitalist who believes in taxing the billionaire class and advocating universal healthcare for all Americans, rather than a Democratic Socialist.) He defeated Stevens by just under 14,000 votes – less than 1 per cent of the overall vote. 

Stevens immediately endorsed El-Sayed and since then, the stars of liberal left, Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, have campaigned for him even as the party machine has thrown its weight behind him. Kamala Harris appeared at an event in Michigan and on Saturday next, former president Barack Obama will join El-Sayed for a rally in Detroit. 

The simple equation on El-Sayed’s chances of edging out Republican candidate Mike Rogers – and therefore maintaining a vital senate seat – is that he needs to win over the traditional black, city-based vote. Michigan blows with the wind in presidential cycles but no Republican has won a US senate seat in Michigan since Spence Abraham in 1994. 

A recent Washington Post-Schar School poll found that of the 83 per cent of black voters who want the Democrats to win control of the senate, 67 per cent would vote for El-Sayed in the Michigan race. Bridging that gap is essential for El-Sayed if he is to win. The reasons for the wariness among black voters are down to a combination of the ubiquitous attack adverts accentuating El-Sayed as a radical candidate, and a simple lack of familiarity: the communities just don’t know him.

During the series of questions from supporters in Flint, Michele Kelly asked El-Sayed why the campaign, and the Democratic Party, was not actively campaigning in black neighbourhoods in cities like Flint.

“I am 67 years old and I don’t think anybody has directly targeted project people,” she told me afterwards.

“I know they haven’t. Knocking on doors. Calling around. I’m not blaming anybody. I say ‘black community’ because that’s how we talk. But it burns me up when they say, ‘the base’. The base of the Democratic Party is the black community. The base of the Republican Party is the white community. Guess who they cover? Them. Guess who the media covers? Them. Guess who gets to go on TV? Them. So, we don’t see no reason ... El-Sayed needs Detroit, yes. But in order to pull an election win off, he needs smaller cities. Like Flint. Which is a black city. 

“This room here did not reflect Flint. At all. Flint is 80 per cent black. White Americans who live in Flint – well, they live in Davison, Burton, Grand Blanc. Most of Flint city itself is black. I thought he did the best he could today. I have been out here trying to encourage family members to pay attention to politics forever. ”

The census statistics on Flint reflect a city still reeling from the rapid contraction of automotive jobs in the city in the 1980s: a median income of $34,000; 34 per cent of residents living below the poverty line; owner-occupier housing at 53 per cent; just 14 per cent with a bachelor’s degree or higher. 

It is a startlingly empty place. But any stranger taking a 20-minute walk through its downtown and the main thoroughfare of Saginaw Street will be struck by buildings that hold stories about its former grandeur. The Durant hotel, an exercise in opulence when it opened in 1919, was the social hub for the 50 years of its existence. Frank Sinatra and Glenn Miller booked in there during the years when Flint was automatic on the tour schedule. It fell into disrepair following its closure and now operates as an apartment complex. 

The Capitol Theatre, designed in the 1920s to emulate the grand Italian opera house style, has been refurbished. A food emporium is housed in what was the printing press of the Flint Journal. Flint Park is a green area now but in the 1920s, it had its own adventure park. On Saginaw Street there are statues to automobile giants, including Billy Durant, the founder of General Motors before he was squeezed out by the financiers and died, in penury, as the operator of a struggling bowling alley in Flint. 

A vast, fenced-off wasteland represents the site of the Buick City along Hamilton avenue, where 28,000 workers clocked in at its peak. Just a thousand jobs remained when the plant closed in 1999. Its premises featured prominently in Roger & Me, the sardonic, evocative documentary by Flint native Michael Moore chronicling the sad closing years of the factory. Michele Kelly graduated from high school in 1977 so she caught the town in its last wave of manufacturing prosperity.

“Yeah, everyone was getting jobs, straight from school. As their parents did. Everyone had new cars, stores everywhere. By the time the next generation came along, General Motors was gone and ten years later, it looked like the Third World. It pisses me off because I remember what it could have been like.”

Flint, then, stands a perfect symbol of Donald Trump’s election promise to somehow reverse the epic monumental decline of the car manufacturing industry. But despite his promises of a resurrection, Flint – and Genesee County – voted for Kamala Harris in 2024. 

It should be promising territory for El-Sayed. At 41, he comes equipped with a formidable range of accomplishments: a professor of epidemiology and Rhodes scholar who worked at the Detroit health department before running for governor of Michigan in 2018, when he lost to Gretchen Whitmer. He has developed an easy, streetwise media articulacy and turns up for campaigns in regulation jeans and casual tops.

Mike Rogers, his Republican opponent, is a survivor of his party’s transformation: a former state senator turned US congressman, he ran against Democrat Elisa Slotkin for Michigan’s other senate seat two years ago and fell short by just 20,000 votes. When Gary Peters, who had held this seat for the Democrats for a full decade, announced his retirement, Trump was in office just eight days. But among his flurry of phone calls was a request to Rogers that he should run again.

“Remember Mike Rogers is running for US senate because Donald Trump called him and asked him to. He won’t really break with him on tariffs, on war, because his only pathway to war is through him,” El-Sayed said on television last weekend.

“Now, why does he want that power so bad? Not because he wants to serve as US senator – he doesn’t have any ideas. He wants that power because the last time he had power he was able to retire and make $14 million as an adviser for the very same corporations he had been regulating as a US congressman. He watched the president make 2.2 billion dollars off the presidency and said: you know what, I gotta get while the getting’s good. And you know who gets got? We do. And all he’s got is to point to me and say ... some scary words and it will work. It’s not going to win. Michiganders are too big for that.”

That may be wishful thinking on his part. All polls depict a race on a knife edge: an early October Insider Advantage poll featuring 1,200 voters surveyed had El-Sayed at 48 per cent to Rogers on 46 per cent, with 5 per cent undecided.

In their highly acrimonious televised debates, Rogers has repeatedly sought to link El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood terrorist group and emphasised his ties to controversial left-wing influencer Hasan Piker. Attack ads on Michigan localised networks introduce him by his full name – Abdulrahman Mohammad El-Sayed before declaring him “the most radical senate candidate in America”.

“When his ally said America deserved 9/11, El-Sayed refused to disavow his remarks,” one advert narrates, referencing Piker, before declaring El-Sayed “too radical, too dangerous, wrong for Michigan”.

Over the course of an hour in St Michael’s Church, El-Sayed roams the room, microphone in hand, trying to debunk the myths and stereotypes. He castigated Rogers for corporate-linked wealth and for owning two yachts.

“Who needs two yachts?” he asks in mock bafflement. He referred to Rogers as a “non-playing character” and referenced Donald Trump’s accented pronunciation of his name.

“Donald Trump can’t seem to take my name out of his mouth. It’s funny because he doesn’t even know how to say it. I mean, to be creepy about Abdul?”

In delivery, he is funny, irreverent and slightly cocky; the northern flipside of the coin to James Talarico’s studied humility.

“This is my first time seeing him live,” Melissa Dugan tells me when the rally ends. “But I did vote for him at the last opportunity I had. Abdul says everything that I am looking for.”

Dugan and her husband run a small business where they live, in Linden, a 20-minute drive from Flint. With one daughter having just graduated from the University of Michigan and their youngest girl currently studying in Michigan State, the last number of years have been a stretch for the family. In addition to running the business, her husband works in real estate while Melissa has a part-time job. Their daughter’s college financial aid was reduced by 30 per cent this year.

“It has made it difficult for us to keep her enrolled. She’s on the dean’s list: she is thriving so we are doing everything we can. We haven’t had health insurance since 2025. Because we can’t afford it. As small business owners we don’t have a company that gives us benefits. 

“So, we have to go through the market place and our health was going to cost $8,000 for the year and it didn’t cover anything and had deductibles. So, we self-insure, which means that if something terrible happens, we hope we can afford it. But I can barely afford my groceries and gas.”

That national cost-of-living crisis, and the sneaking sense that billionaire business interests have subtly hijacked the system has formed a crucial part of El-Sayed’s campaign mission. He has built a formidable funding model despite rejecting corporate and political action committee donations, and one of his vows is to try to wrestle the American electoral system away from the clutches of mega-donor influence.

“It is absolutely insane,” Dugan says of the US health insurance system. “I am all for a socialist government, I am all for Medicare for all. It is ridiculous that as one of the wealthiest countries in the world we don’t have health cover for citizens. 

“This current administration – maybe this sounds extreme – but I really feel part of their goal is just to eliminate much of the lower and middle class. And they will do that by killing us – by making the cost of living so high that we can’t afford to eat or buy medicine.”

We speak for a while about Flint. The city was still in a drift state after the vanishing of General Motors when it was hit with the water crisis in 2014, caused by the cost-saving measure to switch the drinking supply to the Flint river as a source, which was quickly and lastingly contaminated by lead pipes. That civic disaster lasted a full five years, ending just before the pandemic.

The tragedy of Flint is that the people who arrived to make lives and a city there did everything right. They believed, passionately and with confidence, in its future: the proof is there in the surviving architecture and the residential streets that bloomed when Flint’s population climbed as far as 196,000 in the 1960 census. It is home to about 81,000 people now. 

On Saturday afternoon, in gorgeous sunlight, Saginaw Street was completely deserted apart from a lone busker playing guitar and two seniors having a chat on a bench. There are photographs of the same street in Flint’s roaring years: lit up and populated like Sunset Strip and brooking no doubts about its place in the country. Michael Moore’s film drew both lavish praise and considerable pushback for a portrait of a decline that critics felt manipulated the chronology of events to suit the storyline. 

But almost four decades later, the arc of time has validated its broad truth. A once-thriving automotive city was devastated by the reimagining and globalisation of the US industry and the people who still live there have to deal with the aftershocks. There’s something brutal and saddening about its story.

“Flint is a great town with great people,” Melissa Dugan says. “What happened here was none of the citizens’ fault. The system is the problem. And we need huge changes.”

Abdul El-Sayed isn’t the first political aspirant to visit Flint in a campaign year. For decades now, Flint residents have been used to candidates breezing through and issuing passionate words. But El-Sayed is adamant that if he is elected as the first Muslim to sit in the US senate, he will carry Vehicle City with him.

“Flint is the canary in the coal mine,” he said, speaking in the church porch to local television crews after the rally was over.

“You look at the failure of our state government to protect just the basics when it came to water. And Flint was also the place that showed the world what a union could do in terms of a sit-down strike. So, when you think about what Michigan is, Flint ... and Detroit ... they are at the heart of it.”
news.summary: In Flint, birthplace of General Motors, voters wrestling with healthcare costs and economic decline may determine control of the US Senate

news.title: The final lap? Two days on the campaign trail with Trump ahead of US midterm polls
news.text: WASHINGTON: Donald Trump is crisscrossing America to drum up votes for Republican candidates facing tough midterm election races, but the US president's rallies are often hijacked by his basking in the adulation of fervent supporters.AFP followed him on Tuesday and Wednesday during one such trip out West, a rapid succession of flights and rallies -- in a glacial valley in Alaska, on an arid plain in Arizona and in the forests of Montana.The Republican leader is betting on his ability to mobilize voters despite polls predicting that his party will lose control of one or both chambers of Congress on November 3.A Fox News poll released Thursday puts his approval rating at just 36 percent, a new low, largely because of growing dissatisfaction over the cost of living."Please pretend that I am on the ballot," the 80-year-old leader, wearing a red cap, told the crowd Wednesday in Bullhead City, Arizona..Can $1 billion power Republicans to victory in the US midterm elections?.Nostalgia for 2024In 2024, he got nearly 78 percent of the vote in the county where he was speaking in Arizona. The other two counties he visited, in Alaska and Montana, also gave him decisive victories over Democrat Kamala Harris.Donald Trump makes no secret of his preference for traveling to friendly territory, telling reporters that he wants to "pay my respect" to supporters. "We brought back the spirit" of the 2024 presidential campaign, he declared.It is difficult to judge.Each appearance drew committed supporters, the core of his MAGA (Make America Great Again) movement, who are apparently willing to forgive him for soaring fuel prices as well as the war in Iran."The country needs to be a little bit more patient," Theresa Hallesy told AFP on Wednesday in Montana. "There's a lot of stuff going on in the world that he can't control, but he still has to deal with it. I think we're going in the right direction."The 68-year-old retiree waited more than seven hours for Trump to make his entrance into a large rodeo arena commandeered for the occasion.The American president is rallying support for his party, but he seemed almost reluctant to invite local candidates to join him onstage during the tour..Trump went all the way to Alaska in a sign of how close its US Senate race may be.'One minute'"I want you just to come up for one minute because we don't want to hear you for two minutes, three minutes, just one minute," he told Andy Biggs, a conservative seeking to become governor of Arizona.The Republican leader always has one or two announcements tailored to each region.In Alaska on Tuesday, at a hockey rink converted into a rally venue, he laid out his climate-skeptic arguments.In a state whose economy is closely tied to fossil fuels, Trump promoted a major liquefied natural gas project. He also issued presidential pardons for two auto mechanics who were convicted of modifying diesel engines to circumvent emissions regulations.At each rally, Donald Trump promised that every American will receive $5,000 if Republicans retain their majorities in the House of Representatives and the Senate. How this highly controversial proposal, criticized by the opposition, would be funded remains unclear.Yet rather than an electoral offensive, his rallies give the impression of a final tour for a show whose star performer and audience are already feeling nostalgic..Trump's trade wars sting US manufacturers ahead of midterms.Qatari jetIn Montana, thousands of enthusiastic supporters laughed at a now-familiar impersonation of French President Emmanuel Macron and gave Trump a standing ovation as he left the stage, dancing to the ever-present strains of "YMCA."In Arizona, the billionaire delighted the audience with a flyover by the new presidential aircraft, a lavish gift from Qatar.Onstage, he joked about the present, estimated to be worth $400 million: "You know, when you are given gifts, you take them, right?"The joke fell somewhat flat with the audience in a district where both the poverty rate and the unemployment rate are significantly above the national average.The Republican leader then spoke regretfully about the approaching end of his term, saying he has resigned himself to it in "two-and-a-half years. Now a little less than that, sadly.""I said that yesterday and they started screaming, 'Four more years! Four more years!'" Trump continued.He paused. He waited. news.title: Elon Musk Agrees to Settle 2 Lawsuits Over $1 Million Giveaways in 2024 Election
news.text:
Elon Musk and his America PAC agreed in an Oct. 15 court filing to settle two lawsuits alleging that Musk defrauded voters during the 2024 election by promising $1 million giveaways to randomly selected registered voters.

Musk offered the daily giveaways to registered voters who signed a petition supporting both the First and Second Amendments of the Constitution in the weeks leading up to the 2024 presidential election. Two Arizona residents filed lawsuits against Musk and his political action committee (PAC) claiming that while voters were told the $1 million recipients would be chosen randomly in a lottery style, they did not have a real chance to win.

Musk founded America PAC in 2024 to support President Donald Trump’s campaign against Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris.

The plaintiffs in the two proposed class-action lawsuits—Jacqueline McAferty and Joy Harvick—Musk, and America PAC informed U.S. District Judge Robert Pitman of the Western District of Texas’s Austin Division that they reached settlements, which are subject to approval by the court.

The parties requested that the court vacate any deadlines pertaining to the lawsuits and stay further proceedings for 30 days to allow the settlements to be finalized and executed and to file a motion for preliminary approval. Thursday’s court filings did not disclose the terms of the two settlements.

U.S. Magistrate Judge Susan Hightower had said in June that Musk would be required to testify in the lawsuits McAferty v. Musk and Harvick v. Musk.

The two plaintiffs, both Arizona residents, accused Musk and America PAC of misleading voters in seven swing states into signing Musk’s petition to support the Constitution.

The plaintiffs said the defendants promised the $1 million recipients would be selected “randomly.” However, McAferty and Harvick alleged that voters did not have a legitimate chance of winning, citing one of Musk’s lawyers who said the 18 winners were selected because they might be good spokespeople for Musk’s PAC.

McAferty said voters who signed Musk’s petition were required to provide their names, phone numbers, addresses, and email addresses. She told the court that if she had known that she had no chance of winning the $1 million giveaway, she would not have signed the petition or provided her personal information.

McAferty also alleged that Musk and America PAC profited off her personally identifiable information and accused the defendants of defrauding other voters who signed the petition.

Musk and America PAC denied the allegations.

Seeking to dismiss the class-action lawsuits, Musk and his legal team previously said there were multiple “red flags” that showed he had not run an illegal lottery for the $1 million giveaways. Musk’s legal team said voters were informed that the recipients of the $1 million giveaways were “selected to earn” the money and were expected to become spokespeople for America PAC.

However, Pitman said public and promotional statements for the giveaways suggested that Musk and America PAC were “awarding” the money and that the $1 million could be “won.”

“It is plausible that plaintiff justifiably relied on those statements to believe that defendants were objectively offering her the chance to enter a random lottery—even if that is not what they subjectively intended to do,” Pitman wrote in an August court order concerning the McAferty v. Musk case.

The Epoch Times reached out to the plaintiffs’ attorneys for comment on Thursday’s settlement announcements but did not receive a response before publication time. The Epoch Times was unable to reach the attorneys for Elon Musk and America PAC.

The Epoch Times reached out to the plaintiffs’ attorneys for comment on Thursday’s settlement announcements but did not receive a response before publication time. The Epoch Times was unable to reach the attorneys for Elon Musk and America PAC.

news.title: Kansas Dem Adam Hamilton Would Be ‘Out There with People’ if Minneapolis-Style ICE Protests Came to Kansas City
news.text:
Kansas Democrat Senate nominee Adam Hamilton said in January that he would want to be among people protesting if what he was discussing about Minneapolis were happening in Kansas City.

Hamilton, who is challenging incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall (R-KS) in Kansas’s U.S. Senate race, made the comments during a January 22 episode of his Making Sense of Faith with Adam Hamilton podcast.

“I think about on the flip side now — so people who are protesting,” Hamilton said. “And I would just say if there were — I posted on my Facebook page this week something I’d seen from someone else who lives in Minneapolis. Of course that got a lot of comments. But he was kind of just describing what was happening in his community.”

“And I thought if that was happening in Kansas City, I would want to be out there with people,” Hamilton continued.

“You know, I would want to be out there trying to protect — not insulting — with great kindness and compassion and appreciation for ICE agents who are trying to do the right thing,” Hamilton said.

“But if this is being done in a way that’s wrong or, you know, if they’re targeting people because of the color of their skin, or they’re racially profiling people. I think of the two young men in my 7:30 service,” he said.

“I’m going to be standing in front of their house, and I’m hoping there are a whole bunch of other people from our church who are going to stand in front of their house if something like this happened to them,” Hamilton continued. “I don’t believe it would happen to them. But there would be a whole lot of other people, just like in Minneapolis where this is happening.”

Hamilton’s January comments also fit with positions he has taken on immigration over the course of his public career.

“In Scott City, farmers discussed the loss of grain markets to other countries due to the chaos in our markets, and the need for a path to citizenship for hard-working, law-abiding immigrants which help feed the nation by working in ag industries,” Hamilton wrote in a March 10 post about his travels across Kansas.

Hamilton also served on President Barack Obama’s Advisory Council on Faith-based and Neighborhood Partnerships, which addressed immigration in a January 2016 report.

“The failure to provide a path to citizenship for undocumented immigrants has denied countless hardworking people opportunities to earn a living, support their families, and advance their education in this country,” the report stated.

The report also said immigration enforcement could separate parents from their children and create economic hardships for mixed-status families.

Hamilton, the founding and senior pastor of the Church of the Resurrection, also addressed immigration during a 2018 sermon.

“When you see news stories where children are crying, and they’re being taken away from their parents, you should look at those stories in the light of what Jesus said about what happens when you harm children,” Hamilton said after recounting Jesus’s warning that it would be better for someone who harms a child to have “a millstone tied around your neck” and be thrown into the sea than face God’s wrath. 

Breitbart News reported October 14 that Hamilton, who has campaigned as a “different kind of Democrat,” voted for Kamala Harris in 2024 and donated $500 to her campaign on July 23, two days after President Joe Biden ended his reelection bid. Hamilton said he was drawn to Harris by his concern for “the weak, the vulnerable,” called President Donald Trump a “disrupter,” and said January 6 was a “disqualifier” for Trump from his perspective, though he added that he would pray for and try to support Trump after Trump was elected.

news.title: The No-Contact Epidemic Sweeping America
news.text:
No Contact: How a Seductive Ideology Broke Families and Friendships and How We Can Repair Them
By: Noelle Mering
Forum Books, 288 pages, $28

A study from Cornell University recently found that 27 percent of Americans are estranged from a close relative. In many cases, and increasingly so, it is adult children who are estranged from their own parents.

The Ethics and Public Policy Center’s Noelle Mering tackled the phenomenon in a new book published in September, No Contact: How a Seductive Ideology Broke Families and Friendships and How We Can Repair Them. Mering brilliantly diagnoses the many cultural maladies that have created this situation, and offers hope and good advice to those in estranged situations.

Earlier this month, the issue of parental estrangement received some attention when an aggrieved grandmother asked Florida Rep. Byron Donalds what he would do about “grandparents’ rights.” She complained that she hadn’t seen her grandchild in a few weeks and said that she was working with her local representative “to see if we could do a federal law so [grandparents’ rights] could be nationwide.” Just from the woman’s annoying tone of voice, which reeked of entitlement, you could tell that, at least in this situation, the parent rather than the adult child was probably at fault.

But let’s be real: in most cases of estrangement these days in the United States, the majority of the blame lies with the adult child. That seems to be the perspective of Mering, though she doesn’t entirely let parents off the hook.

Mering explains the five “core conditions” driving the phenomenon of parental estrangement: “(1) demythologizing the family, (2) social hygiene, (3) broadening the definition of trauma, (4) the infallibility narrative, and (5) cultural narcissism,” and I am thoroughly convinced by her diagnosis.

At the root of these five conditions, writes Mering, is “a radical revision of what it means to be human” that “recast[s] the person around two opposing principles: the exaltation of autonomy and the incentivization of victimhood.”

Here are her five core conditions:

1. “Demythologizing the Family”: The Bible commands us: “Honor thy father and mother.” Mering informs us that radical progressivism teaches something entirely different. In its understanding, the Bible’s morality of demanding special obligations toward one’s family in fact functions to “hide oppression, abuse, and other toxic behavior.” Therefore, progressives seek to “demythologize the family” by dismantling the supposed “myth” that one’s family is worthy of special regard. In a culture in which family is supposedly arbitrary, and in which moral demands to them only “serve harmful power interests,” one is better off prioritizing oneself as an individual and therefore casting aside one’s obligations toward one’s parents.

2. “Social Hygiene”: In an age of identity politics, people increasingly “evaluate a person’s character, and therefore their social acceptability, based on political tribe.” In this environment, many a progressive young person decides their parents are immoral because they are aligned with political conservatism. This is exacerbated by progressivism’s tendency to have a “dynamic of low differentiation,” that is, a low tolerance for those with convictions different from one’s own. The combination of judging people’s character based on their political tribe and having a low tolerance for those with different beliefs leads, Mering argues, to “social hygiene,” meaning “scrubbing our social circles clean of toxic ideas by cutting contact with those who hold them.” 

3. “Broadening the Definition of Trauma”: People once understood trauma as stemming only from things as severe as war and physical abuse. Now, however, anything can be traumatic. A parent telling you to do your laundry when you’re 12 can lead to “trauma.” Mering explains that many of the parents she spoke with who experienced estrangement from their children had made missteps as parents, but “theirs were the ordinary parental failings that, in previous generations, would have been absorbed or forgiven rather than collected, catalogued, and marshaled retroactively to support a narrative of childhood harm.” When young people are told on social media and with their therapists that ordinary experiences of hardship and imperfect familial relationships are traumatic, they “search for [trauma] in their own lives, and perhaps even retroactively project it onto their past.”

4. “The Infallibility Narrative”: Mering explains to us that there are copious social media influencers, on TikTok in particular, who essentially cheer on their viewers in cutting off contact with their parents. One such person is Patrick Teahan. In one video recounted by Mering, Teahan asserts that parents who push back against their adult child’s decision to cut off all contact are proving just how toxic they are: “When estranged parents reactively believe that their child has been wrongfully influenced by a therapist or whatever, by TikTok or whatever, it kinda implies that the child has no … thoughts of their own and that … the parents [see] them as an object and not as an individual. It’s kind of like a clue.” Of course, as Mering points out, any parent who has been wrongfully estranged will of course push back against their child’s decision. But in the progressive mindset, an adult child who estranges themselves from their parents must necessarily be right. This is the “infallibility narrative”: “Parents who have been cut off and tell their stories online are regularly subjected to derision and armchair psychoanalysis, while adult children are almost unanimously affirmed in their decision in such forums.” It is, writes Mering, a philosophy of “Believe all adult children” that is akin to “Believe all women.” In this environment, young people are very much cheered on to cut off their family.

5. “Cultural Narcissism”: Mering points us to Christopher Lasch’s 1979 book The Culture of Narcissism, which posits that the rise of individualism and consumerism leads to, as she puts it, “widespread narcissistic behavior.” Lasch’s predictions proved true, Mering writes, in that narcissistic traits have risen dramatically in the United States since the time that book was written. Between 1979 and 2006, narcissistic traits, like a focus on money, fame, and image, rose while empathy declined. A further study carried out for the Financial Times between 2014 and 2025 found a huge rise in neurotic traits such as “emotional fragility and self-preoccupation” and a corresponding decrease in agreeableness.

This is where both sides — adult children and parents — are at fault. While this rise in narcissistic traits is “most pronounced” in young people, older Americans have also been sucked into this narcissism. Mering writes: “The cultural currents fueling narcissism and emotional fragility affect us all, not only the younger generation nor the ideologically possessed. Family breakdown didn’t begin with Gen Z; its logic has been unfolding for decades.”

This can be seen most clearly in the drastic rise in divorce rates in the latter half of the 20th century. “The normalization of divorce has communicated a quiet but devastating message: Family members are replaceable,” she writes. “We can’t sit comfortably within a culture that treats divorce casually and then condemn young people for ‘divorcing’ their families.”

Mering spoke to a psychoanalyst, Erica Komisar, about this problem of narcissistic traits. Komisar told Mering: “The repercussions of three generations of self-centeredness means parents are modeling selfishness and emotional fragility to their children. The shift in values to a more self-focused parenting style is contributing to a rise in disorders of the self, otherwise known as narcissistic disorders.” This phenomenon, Mering explains, is made worse by social media.

With the rise of narcissistic traits and systemic divorce, some of these parents are, in fact, bad parents. That grandma who told Byron Donalds she was working with her congressman to make a federal law that would force her daughter to let her see her grandchild is probably an example of that.

But young people’s increasing propensity to prioritize their feelings over everyone else is the real problem today. In our culture of selfishness, Mering writes, “Every person becomes the sole author of themselves, bound by nothing higher than the demand to be true to themselves.” This is a very dangerous pathology, and it is one many young people are succumbing to.

I once attended a brunch in which the women, all in their 20s, spoke about how they learned when they became adults that their parents had made tons of mistakes and were deeply flawed. They warned me that soon I would realize all the many faults with my parents. I told them that no, that wasn’t the case for me; my parents are wonderful parents. Just wait, they told me, and you’ll see that they’re actually bad. They were, of course, wrong, but the sentiment expressed is deeply worrying. Young people are collectively deciding that all the members of the older generations traumatized us and emotionally abused us.

Noelle Mering does an excellent job setting out how this pathology seeped into our culture, how it manipulates people into destroying their families, and what we can do about it. We’re well-served by learning from her.

news.title: Iowa’s independent Trump voters are mad as hell — but still probably won’t vote Democratic
news.text:
For the third installment of MS NOW’s “The Voter Files,” we went to West Des Moines to hear from two groups of reluctant Trump voters — one group from the city’s suburbs and another from small towns and rural areas. Most have split their tickets in past elections.

Of the three states we’ve visited so far, Iowa offers Democrats the clearest and most hopeful picture. In Maine, Republican Sen. Susan Collins’ standing as a long-tenured institution may help her withstand Democratic momentum. In Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed’s struggles with some of his party’s traditional constituencies have kept the race tight.

But in Iowa, Democrats have taken the national distrust of Trump’s self-dealing and pointed it at Republican Senate candidate Ashley Hinson, raising questions about how her wealth has grown since she entered Congress. ​​The resulting cynicism may give Democrat Josh Turek enough of an edge to win: enough crossover votes and enough depressed Republican turnout.

Low marks for Trump

Elise Jordan moderates a focus group of Iowan Trump voters on October 9, 2026.

National polls show President Donald Trump at the lowest approval of his second term, and the Iowans we met were no more generous. All of them said they were unenthusiastic about voting for him in 2024. Asked to rate his second term on a scale of one to 10, none went higher than a six, most gave him a four or a five, and the lowest assessment was a two.

“Five is almost too generous,” said Diane, an independent. “He has a lot of room for improvement.”

One participant called him “unhinged.” Another described his second term as “a personal session, like his playground.”

For these voters, the clearest evidence of broken promises is the cost of living. Consumer prices are up 3.7% over the past year.

“Our prices were going to come down. Cost of living was going to get easier,” said Janella, a Republican. “Still haven’t seen it.”

Then there’s Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran. In national polling, only roughly 34% of Americans say Trump’s decision to go to war was the right one. He promised no new wars, and when he took office in January 2025, the United States wasn’t at war. Now, voters see not only continuing conflicts in Ukraine and Gaza, but a new war with Iran that Trump launched.

“It seems like we’re in more wars than ever before,” said Tim, an independent.

Jack, another independent, tied the broken promise to avoid war to rising costs.

“I think we’re paying for that at the gas pump, grocery store, etc.,” he said. Gas prices have jumped 34% over the past year, and groceries prices are up around 2.5%.

They’d do it again

Elise Jordan moderates a focus group of Iowan Trump voters on October 9, 2026.

These voters went into Trump’s second term with their eyes open. Some dreaded a return to the drama of his first term and voted for him anyway.

“Do I really want to deal with all the drama that comes with him?” said Kristi, an independent, recalling her decision in 2024. “But then, what was my other choice?”

“He’s gotten worse,” Janella said, describing a president who has dropped any pretense of working with his own party, let alone with Democrats.

Yet for all their misgivings, when asked whether they would change their 2024 votes, all but one agreed they would vote for him again over Kamala Harris.

“There were no other options,” said Dirk, a right-leaning independent, raising his hand.

It’s this sentiment — that they would choose Trump again — that helps explain why Trump’s sagging approval hasn’t translated into decisive Democratic leads in some battleground states.

Two years later, what drives these voters as they weigh their Senate and House options is less Trump himself than a broader distrust of politics.

Kate, an independent, offered the most charitable view of Trump’s presidency.

“At least he is trying,” she said. “At least he is pushing a button somewhere.”

In theory, that’s a low bar for the opposition to clear. But these voters don’t see a compelling alternative from Democrats, or any vision that convinces them the party would do better.

No home with Democrats?

Elise Jordan moderates a focus group of Iowan voters on October 9, 2026.

“Right now, we're stuck with a Republican Party that will do nothing to offend Trump, and a Democratic Party that will do nothing except try to go after Trump, any way, shape, or form,” Dirk said. “So in the end, we all get screwed.”

The Iowans echoed what we heard from similar voters in Maine and Michigan: Democrats seem unmoored, fixated on Trump and short on concrete policy. Most alienating of all is their sense that Democrats look down on them for voting for Trump.

“I feel like they all think that we're like racist,” Chandler said. “It's like they always think that we're all against everything. It's just their agenda that they try to push on us.”

Some said those assumptions about their motives ignore the real circumstances and needs that shaped their votes.

“Personally, my vote was motivated by potential changes that Trump could make to the economy,” Anne said.

Democrats, Janella argued, were not paying attention to their lived reality.

“They need to stop all the fighting and bickering amongst themselves, and really genuinely take a good look at what the American people are dealing with,” Janella said. “This is our livelihood we're talking about, and every single politician has forgotten about that.”

Will they skip the Senate race?

Elise Jordan moderates a focus group of Iowan voters on October 9, 2026.

Disenchanted with Republicans and unconvinced by Democrats, some of the Iowans we met are weighing not who to support in the Senate race, but whether to vote in it at all.

The two groups split sharply. Of the 10 rural and small-town voters, six are leaning toward Hinson and four are considering Turek. None of the 10 suburban voters is considering Hinson; seven said they would leave the Senate race blank, and the other three are considering Turek.

Focus groups aren’t polls, and 20 voters can’t predict a statewide race. But if the 2024 electorate turns out again and that pattern holds in suburbs and small towns across Iowa, Turek could be well positioned to win. He wouldn’t need to convert Trump voters wholesale, just persuade some to cross over and many others to skip the race.

For Hinson, the danger isn’t that these voters have embraced Democrats. It’s that they’ve given up.

“You just lose all faith in everybody eventually because nothing gets done, and you lose trust and become cynical,” Jack said.
news.author: Ja’han Jones

news.title: Trump’s diesel deal with Russia is ‘America First’
news.text:
President Trump struck a deal last week for Russia to supply diesel immediately to the U.S. to lower the sky-high prices that Americans are paying for this essential fuel. Truckers, farmers and ranchers are being hit the hardest by the sharp increase in diesel prices, and this cost is passed on to all who rely on trucks for the shipment of goods, which is nearly everyone.

The price today of filling a commercial fuel tank is $1,000 or more in many parts of our country. Russia is the No. 2 supplier of diesel to the world, after the United States, and the sanctions against Russian sales of diesel during its war with Ukraine have driven up the costs of groceries and much else.

“I made the right choice for the American People – ALWAYS, AMERICA FIRST!” Trump responded on Truth Social to his critics. Globalist Republicans, including Sens. John Curtis, R-Utah, and Thom Tillis, R-N.C., and Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb., have spoken out against Trump about this, but they have squawked against MAGA policies before, as did Curtis’s predecessor Mitt Romney.

Trump points out that the European Union, which continues to provoke Russia by pushing to bring Ukraine into the EU, has paid Russia $250 billion for energy, and yet the “fake news media doesn’t want to get near that story.”

On Tuesday, the EU is opening new negotiations with Ukraine for it to join as a member, which is why Russia continues to fight. The U.S. has reportedly been providing intelligence to Ukraine about Russian movements and targets, but Trump has threatened to suspend that assistance while also calling for a new presidential election in Ukraine to replace Zelensky.

The last presidential election in Ukraine was held more than seven years ago, on April 21, 2019, when oligarchs pushed this professional comedian into office. Zelensky failed to give many interviews for that office as presidential candidates normally do, and instead shirked the press and traditional forums that would have at least helped him learn what is necessary for the job.

While Zelensky did not attend campaign events in Ukraine and has refused to allow another presidential election, he did find time to campaign for Kamala Harris in Pennsylvania in 2024, attending one of her events as she attempted to defeat Trump. Many voters of Ukrainian descent live in Pennsylvania and also Ohio, but Trump won both states, including Ohio by a landslide.

Monday marked the 1,693rd day of the Russian invasion of Ukraine, which began under the presidency of Joe Biden. Trump campaigned on ending this war as soon as possible, and he has made every attempt to do so but has not received sufficient cooperation from Zelensky and Europe.

In key battleground states like Iowa, affordable diesel fuel is essential for farmers and others to be able to ship their goods for sale throughout the rest of our big country. Diesel peaked at $6.528 per gallon in the United States a few weeks ago and has come down a bit since then thanks in part to Trump.

Republicans are struggling to hold onto statewide seats in the heartland of America. A Democrat is ahead in Iowa’s governor’s race, despite how that office has been held by Republicans for 15 years, and its U.S. Senate race is considered a toss-up.

High diesel prices came up in the debate between the telegenic Republican candidate for Senate, Ashley Hinson, and her tenacious Democrat opponent, Josh Turek. Hinson is a former newscaster and congresswoman, while Turek is a state representative and former professional wheelchair basketball player.

Turek is running a social media ad featuring a farmer hit hard by fuel prices. Meanwhile, Hinson said in the debate that the war in the Middle East must end soon, which the Republican candidate for U.S. Senate Mike Rogers has also called for in Michigan.

Trump is right that Americans should not be burdened with higher energy costs due to the perpetual war between Russia and Ukraine. Diesel prices are roughly 65% to 71% higher than a year ago, which is more than twice the increase in the price of gasoline during the same time period.

Ukrainian officials ask what they are getting in return for Trump relaxing the diesel sanctions on Russia, but the U.S. has already sent hundreds of billions of dollars in cash and military supplies to Ukraine, along with crucial military intelligence. Americans have received nothing in exchange for all this.

Americans should not be forced to fund, through inflation, the globalist scheme to make Ukraine part of the EU, which Russia is fighting to stop. If European leaders at the EU insist on continuing to antagonize Russia, they should bear the costs of that rather than burdening Americans.
news.summary: 'Americans should not be forced to fund, through inflation, the globalist scheme to make Ukraine part of the EU'

news.title: Ashley Hinson's Race vs. Josh Turek Tightens as Trump Plans Iowa Rallies
news.text: A new Marist poll that released on Thursday shows that Republican Ashley Hinson is gaining on Democrat Josh Turek in the race for Iowa's U.S. Senate seat as President Donald Trump plans to visit the Hawkeye State next week. Iowa is among this year's most competitive Senate races, as Turek and Hinson vie for the open seat left by retiring Republican Senator Joni Ernst. Polls continue to show a tight race between the two candidates after their first debate last week, where tariffs, immigration and voting records played a major role. A second debate was held on Tuesday night, where again the candidates sparred over Iran, tariffs and immigration. The poll offers new insight into the close race only weeks from Election Day. While a September poll by Marist found Turek with an 8-point lead over Hinson, the gap has narrowed significantly between the two as Thursday's poll put Turek only 3 points ahead. Newsweek reached out to the campaigns for Turek and Hinson via email for comment on Thursday. Trump Schedules Iowa Rallies: What We Know Trump has planned two Iowa rallies in the coming weeks, aiming to boost Hinson's campaign against Turek. He has already endorsed Hinson, a U.S. Representative, for the Senate race. The Iowa rallies are the most recent in a series of campaign stops Trump has made ahead of the fast-approaching midterms as Republicans fight to maintain their majority in the U.S. Senate amid several tight races, including in Alaska and Texas. Trump is set to visit Iowa on October 22 and November 1. “I just got off the phone with President Trump," Republican Party of Iowa Chair Jeff Kaufmann said in a statement, according to a report by The Des Moines Register. "He told me that he will be in Iowa on October 22 and November 1. He is anxious for Iowans to hear his message before they vote. Stay tuned for further details." Times and venues for the rallies have not been announced. Ashley Hinson vs. Josh Turek: Latest Polls Two new polls came out this week assessing the race between Hinson and Turek. The polls were conducted by YouGov and Marist. The YouGov poll, which was held from October 6 to October 12, surveyed 2,245 likely voters and found that 47 percent planned to vote for Turek, giving him a 1-point lead over Hinson. According to the poll, 41 percent of respondents backed former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024, compared with 52 percent who voted for Trump. Given Turek's edge, the results suggest he has won support from at least some voters who previously cast ballots for Trump. The Marist poll released on Thursday was held from October 8 to October 11 and surveyed 1,100 likely voters. Turek also leads Hinson in this poll, by 3 points. However, his lead over Hinson is much narrower than the last Marist poll, released in September, which gave him an 8-point lead. The study by Marist also showed improvement in Trump's approval ratings across Iowa. The September Marist poll showed that 41 percent of registered voters in Iowa approved of the job Trump was doing in office while 58 percent disapproved. A month later, 44 percent said they approved, while 53 percent disapproved. Biggest Issues Facing Iowa Voters Iowa voters are most concerned about the economy amid inflation and surging gas prices, according to a poll by The Economist that surveyed 650 likely voters on October 5 and October 6. The economy led top issues for voters, at 42 percent. It was followed by healthcare at 18 percent, threats to democracy at 10 percent and education at 8 percent. This year's midterm elections could flip control of the House and Senate as Republican candidates work to overcome widespread American concerns tied to the economy, inflation, rising fuel costs and the Iran war. Although Iowa has voted Republican in the Senate elections since 2008, the state has also had a history of voting for presidential candidates from both political parties, making the current political environment a competitive one. Trump won Iowa the last three election cycles, but before that, former President Barack Obama won the state twice. When Is Early Voting in Iowa? Early voting began in Iowa on October 14 and will continue through November 2. The election is November 3. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Kate Nalepinski and Edward T. Cummins
news.summary: Republican Ashley Hinson is gaining on Democrat Josh Turek in the race for Iowa's U.S. Senate seat, a new poll shows.
news.author: Anna Skinner

news.title: Kamala Harris Slams Biden and Trump Administrations for Failing to Act 'More Forcefully' Against Israel
news.text:
Former Vice President Kamala Harris said that both the Biden and Trump administrations failed to use U.S. leverage "sooner and more forcefully" to curb what she called the Israeli government's "horrific conduct" in the war in Gaza, RadarOnline.com has learned.

Speaking at the Asan Institute for Policy Studies, Harris said the United States has at times fallen short of its "moral obligation to human rights and international law."Harris Calls Out Both Biden and Trump AdministrationsShe claimed that the alleged "failure" to act offered Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu "a blank check."

The remarks came during a speech on American leadership, alliances, trade and the need to hold partners accountable for their share of global defense.

Harris argued that Washington must be willing to confront allies when their actions conflict with human rights and international law.Harris Wrote About Biden in MemoirThis isn't the first time she's shared criticism of the Biden administration's behavior regarding Israel.

In her 2025 memoir, 107 Days, she wrote that she had "pleaded with Joe" to extend the same empathy he showed Ukrainians to innocent Gazan civilians, but that his remarks on Palestinian suffering "came off as inadequate and forced."

She also wrote that Netanyahu had wanted Trump rather than Biden in the White House and had undermined Biden's loyalty to Israel.

During the 2024 campaign, Harris balanced calls for an immediate cease-fire and concern over civilian casualties with repeated statements that Israel had a right to defend itself.Harris Could Be Running Again in 2028Harris has said she has not decided whether she will run for president again in 2028. 

She leads or runs near the top of most early Democratic primary polls, though no major candidate has formally declared.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom has said he would not run if Harris enters the race, calling a contest between two Californians a disadvantage for both.Voters Will Have Loaded Democratic PrimaryOther frequently discussed potential contenders include Michigan Gov. news.title: Cold weather and high prices could flip the Senate
news.text:
This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day. Subscribe here.
Throughout his second term, President Donald Trump has saddled his party with no shortage of political liabilities — from the mass pardons of January 6 convictions to ICE killings of US citizens to questionable Reflecting Pool redesign choices.
For voters, however, there is one stain on Trump’s record more unsightly than all the rest: his failure to reduce Americans’ cost of living.
As the midterm campaign enters its home stretch, Americans’ expenses are rising — and the GOP’s prospects are consequently dimming.
Last month, consumer prices were 3.7 percent higher than they had been one year earlier, according to a Consumer Price Index report released on Wednesday. That represented an acceleration in the inflation rate, one driven largely by skyrocketing fuel prices: Gasoline was 9.1 percent more expensive in September than it had been in August. As a result, America’s average real wage has fallen by 44 cents since January.
In less than three weeks, Americans will head to the polls to decide which party controls Congress, along with a slew of state and local offices. As we count down to that momentous and potentially messy day, this newsletter is partnering with our colleague Astead Herndon and Vox’s The Midterms, Actually team for weekly editions on the biggest issues shaping the midterms. We’re breaking down one issue each week and suggesting further reading and races to watch in November.
Last week, we tackled the data center backlash. And this week, we’re digging into affordability.
Go a little deeper
[Media: https://www.datawrapper.de/_/fpHba/]
These upward trends in prices aren’t lost on voters. In a recent Pew Research survey, just 21 percent of Americans said economic conditions were “excellent” or “good” — while 65 percent said that Trump’s policies had made the economy worse.
The high cost of living is weighing on Republican candidates in all battleground races. Maine provides just one example of how potent the issue could prove on Election Day.
From one angle, the state’s Senate race might seem like a gimme for Democrats. Kamala Harris won Maine by nearly 7 points in 2024. Thus, in 2026 — when Democrats are poised to win in a national landslide — one might expect the party to easily triumph.
But Republican incumbent Susan Collins is an unusually formidable foe. The race has been a dead heat, with Democratic nominee Troy Jackson leading by just 2 points in a recent Suffolk University poll.
Fortunately for Jackson, Mainers’ energy bills are expected to soar in the campaign’s final weeks, plausibly increasing voters’ appetite for change in the process. 
Maine is America’s second coldest state and unusually reliant on oil for home heat. As autumn advances, its residents will use more heating oil, thereby driving up both their personal bills and market prices. Thanks to the global energy crunch, a gallon of such fuel is already nearly twice as expensive as it was this time last year. 
Jackson has been hitting Collins on the issue relentlessly. That could put a chill in Collins’s reelection odds — and thus, the GOP’s hopes of retaining Senate control.
